## 3. System-by-system comparison: unintended input filtering vs. intentional gesture

### 3.1 Ableton Live — rejection by loudness, not by tremor

The Velocity device's three out-of-range modes (Clip / Gate / Fixed) act on each note in isolation; Gate silently discards notes below `Lowest`. The "Random" parameter injects jitter, which is the opposite of what a tremor user needs (https://www.ableton.com/en/live-manual/12/live-midi-effect-reference/; https://obedia.com/how-to-use-the-velocity-midi-effect-in-ableton-live/). The complementary Note Length and Pitch MIDI effects can also shape timing and pitch-bleed artifacts. None carry latency budgets or confidence scores; they are deterministic MIDI math. Novation's own support documentation recommends capping `Out Hi` for Launchpad velocity (https://support.novationmusic.com/hc/en-gb/articles/206689619-Limiting-note-velocity-in-Launchpad-User-mode-in-Ableton-Live). Third-party "Simple Threshold MIDI Device" devices block notes under a set value (https://blog.abletondrummer.com/midi-velocity-control-in-ableton/).

Ableton's accessibility surface (Live 12) — screen-reader compatibility, Tab-navigation, Speak Help Text, high-contrast theme, and expanded keyboard shortcuts (https://help.ableton.com/hc/en-us/articles/11550373507868-Accessibility-in-Live-Overview; https://www.ableton.com/en/live-manual/12/accessibility-and-keyboard-navigation/) — is described by Ableton's staff as "a lifeline for many music producers, particularly those with motor skill disabilities" (https://www.musicradar.com/news/ableton-live-accessibility-revolution; https://umatechnology.org/with-live-12-ableton-knocked-accessibility-out-of-the-park/), but no tremor filter is claimed anywhere.

### 3.2 Logic Pro — Smart Controls are macros, not tremor compensation

The only Logic-side remediation that overlaps with tremor is **macOS Mouse Keys** (numeric-keypad cursor emulation) and Slow Keys / Sticky Keys / Switch Control — all host-OS features, not Logic features (https://support.apple.com/content/dam/edam/applecare/images/en_US/otherassets/accessibility/vpat_logic_pro_2024.pdf). Practitioners seeking tremor accommodation in Logic overwhelmingly rely on (a) external hardware with their own anti-tremor firmware, (b) host-level assistive tools like SteadyMouse on Windows or built-in macOS pointer smoothing, and (c) tracks of pre-quantized MIDI rather than live performance capture.

### 3.3 SteadyMouse — direct, but cursor-level

Documented features relevant to creative work include a filter strength slider with the explicit tuning procedure, **click-duration gating** that drops mouse clicks shorter than a configurable threshold (distinguishing accidental taps from intentional ones by hold time), an **Icon Targeting** snap-to-target mode that lets a user double-tap a modifier key to commit to the nearest clickable element, and a **Num-Lock (or Scroll-Lock) global on/off toggle** so a user can switch back to raw cursor input when doing fine calibrated work such as editing automation curves (https://www.steadymouse.com/manual/). SteadyMouse's limits are clear: it cannot distinguish intentional vibrato-like mid-pitch MIDI modulation from involuntary 4–7 Hz oscillation because it has no notion of musical intent. That distinction has to happen further up the stack — in the DAW or in a custom MIDI effect.

## 4. HCI research on pathological tremor vs. musical vibrato

### 4.1 Frequency-band separation is close to a hard constraint

The literature consistently reports that the discriminating features are not rate but regularity, shape, and context: vibrato is sinusoidal and periodic; tremor is more variable and often superimposed on intentional motion (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5392085/; https://exa.ai/library/publication/3fjs73lrd3d).

### 4.2 What an algorithm can — and cannot — infer

A representative tremor vs. vibrato separation framework appears in Boeck, Widmer et al. (ISMIR 2013), "Local Group Delay based Vibrato and Tremolo Suppression for Onset Detection." Their weighting of spectral-flux onset detection by local group delay reduces false onsets caused by vibrato/tremolo energy peaks by **up to 50%** across three corpora: 25,927 mixed onsets, 7,677 violin onsets, and 1,448 opera-singer onsets (https://www.cp.jku.at/research/papers/Boeck_Widmer_Ismir_2013.pdf). Note that this is the *opposite* direction from what a tremor user needs — they want vibrato-style modulation to *pass through*, but the algorithm is built to treat both as spurious onsets. Reusing this for tremor accommodation would require inverting the cost function.

For EMG-level discrimination (closer to what a MIDI exoskeleton might exploit), the Missouri group showed that the **frequency of EMG modulation in ET shifts when voluntary motion is initiated** vs. when the patient is merely holding posture — a "tremor frequency based filter" using an STFT-derived switch achieved partial voluntary-motion preservation that pure low-pass filters damaged (http://vigir.ee.missouri.edu/~gdesouza/Research/Conference_CDs/BioRob_2012/files/0452.pdf). The same group's "optimal digital filtering for tremor suppression" introduced an "equalizer" framework for joystick teleoperation, validated both on artificially-induced vibration and a Parkinson's subject (https://nemours.elsevierpure.com/en/publications/optimal-digital-filtering-for-tremor-suppression/).

The most mature algorithmic work is the **Weighted-Frequency Fourier Linear Combiner (WFLC)** from Carnegie Mellon (Riviere, Hsu, Thakor, 1995–1996; https://publications.ri.cmu.edu/storage/publications/pub_files/pub3/riviere_cameron_1995_2/riviere_cameron_1995_2.pdf). WFLC estimates tremor frequency and amplitude in real time using a truncated Fourier series model, then subtracts the tremor component with **zero phase lag** — critical for preserving timing of voluntary motion — and achieved "average rms amplitude reduction of 69%" in active tremor compensation (https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~micron/filtering.htm). The **StylPen** system implemented WFLC in real-time pen input and tested it with pathological tremor subjects writing cursive, with "results favorable to the handwriting using StylPen and its WFLC filtering algorithm" (https://doi.org/10.1109/nebc.1996.503243). The **Enhanced BMFLC (E-BMFLC)** was validated on 14 PD and 13 ET patients across three degrees of freedom, showing it "significantly enhances the accuracy in comparison with the performance of conventional BMFLC filtering" and "significantly reduces the sensitivity to parameter tuning and intrapatient variabilities" (https://doi.org/10.1109/jstsp.2016.2530632). The key limitation for musical applications: WFLC assumes tremor is quasi-periodic noise to be subtracted; if a musician intentionally performs vibrato at 5 Hz and their pathological tremor is also at 5 Hz, the algorithm cannot distinguish them based on frequency alone.

The **TRECEY algorithm** (2025; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41190944/) uses eye-tracking data to stabilize cursor movement for PD patients during multimedia interaction, bypassing the tremor/musical intent problem entirely via an alternative input modality. A 2025 *Scientific Reports* smart-pen paper compares Fx-LMS, Fx-NLMS, Fx-LMS/NLMS hybrid, RLS, and Kalman filtering on real PD signals from the NewHandPD dataset, finding that **RLS achieves the lowest mean squared error, but the Kalman Filter converges approximately eight times faster** — relevant because convergence speed translates directly to user-perceived latency during composition (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-14196-5).

A 2025 gesture-based DMI study found that "participants learn the system quickly: between the first and fourth performance, there was a **73% reduction in errors** and a **22% decrease in mean time per note**" (https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3750069.3750438).

The **XPadInput VibratoIntentDetector** proposal (https://github.com/sp80808/XPadInput/issues/27) represents the closest existing framework to the specific problem of tremor-vs-vibrato discrimination in MIDI capture. It derives vibrato energy from raw motion magnitude and notes that "a broad one-off tilt, controller repositioning or transient recoil can create periodic pitch modulation even though the physical gesture was not periodic." The proposed solution combines alternating sign/zero-crossing structure, inter-reversal timing consistency, autocorrelation at plausible vibrato periods, band-limited periodic energy, and movement amplitude thresholds — not yet clinically validated with pathological tremor populations. The **EMPiano** system (https://github.com/HCUM/empiano) takes a different approach: EMG to detect a specific finger-wiggle gesture and map it to pitch vibrato, bypassing positional tremor entirely at the signal level.

CMU's work on extracting command gestures from continuous musician motion (https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~rbd/papers/Extracting-Commands-CMMR-2013.pdf) combines a gesture threshold model with Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) for real-time gesture spotting, using automatic threshold selection based on F-measure evaluation — directly relevant to the tremor/expressive gesture boundary problem.

### 4.3 Gesture rejection HCI: the Voight-Kampff Machine as the closest analogue

The cleanest HCI work on thresholding tremor-like vs. intentional motion is Taranta et al.'s **Voight-Kampff Machine (VKM)**, CHI 2022 (https://cs.ucf.edu/~jjl/pubs/Taranta2022.pdf). VKM is not a tremor filter; it is a *rejection-threshold selector* for custom-gesture recognizers that must decide which continuous-stream inputs to accept as gestures vs. treat as non-gesture noise. The relevance is direct: any system that filters "the wobble" must decide where the wobble ends and the gesture begins.

Key quantitative findings: VKM is the **only threshold-selection technique that consistently achieves high accuracy across four input device types** (pen, mouse, 3D-depth, IMU) on the high-activity gesture datasets tested. Taranta et al. write: "loose boundaries can lead to high false positive rates and degrade user experience"; "eliminating false positives is more important than eliminating false negatives" (citing Katsuragawa et al., reference [21] in their paper). A false positive here is the *same failure mode* as a tremor spike passing through to a note. VKM's technical contribution is a synthetic-data technique ("Mincer") that produces **negative samples near the gesture boundary**, yielding tighter rejection thresholds than prior splicing techniques. Empirical tuning parameters: training-set size shrinks the threshold (more positive examples → tighter cut); gesture-production variability widens it (gaming/performance contexts are more variable than desktop data-collection contexts, sometimes substantially so). Mapping VKM to vibrato preservation would require representing both tremor and vibrato in the same feature space and tuning VKM to prefer the more periodic of the two.

## 5. Documented case studies of musicians with movement disorders

### 5.1 Samuel Smith — Parkinson's, AI-mediated workflow (2026)

London-based singer-songwriter Samuel Smith, diagnosed with Parkinson's in 2020, released *The Art of Letting Go* in 2026. Smith hums melodies into a phone, uploads them to **Suno** and **Udio**, and edits the AI-generated demos into the final album's instrumental plan. He reports needing **"50, 100, 150 attempts"** per demo before producing something usable (https://fortune.com/2026/05/30/parkinsons-ai-music-humming-demos/; https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/05/30/world/ai-helped-musician-with-parkinsons-finish-new-album-when-he-could-no-longer-play-guitar/; https://aitoolsobserver.com/hub/ai-for-musicians-with-disabilities-inside-samuel-smiths-workflow-with-suno-and-udio/). The AI demos were translation layers between his humming and session musicians, not the final masters. This sidesteps the tremor-vs-intent problem by removing the tremor-bearing input modality entirely.

### 5.2 Kira — Essential Tremor, DBS

A touring musician profiled by PMD Alliance in December 2025 reports that prior to deep-brain stimulation she "couldn't play her guitar, and times when she couldn't even get on stage," and that she historically self-medicated with alcohol because prescriptions failed. After a 30 October 2024 DBS procedure, "Immediately, I saw improvement in my right hand. I cried on the operating table as I watched a hand that I felt so disconnected with… show a steadiness" (https://www.pmdalliance.org/2025/12/03/touring-musician-kiras-essential-tremor-journey/). This is a hardware/neurosurgical remediation case, not a DAW-software one — but it documents the magnitude of the symptom set software systems are working against.

### 5.3 Valerie Bryan — Essential Tremor, MRgFUS candidate

A Scottish trad musician with ET published in TRACS (https://tracscotland.org/blog/essential-tremor-a-musicians-perspective-by-valerie-bryan/) documents progressive loss of capability: "I can no longer play the flute or whistle, as I can't really get them to my mouth, let alone hold them there, or play them. (I can still play the piano a bit, and sing, though – I'm lucky!)." She was awaiting Magnetic Resonance-guided Focused Ultrasound treatment. The blog explicitly enumerates DAW-relevant tremor impairments: "playing musical instruments, … using a computer… Carrying cups/mugs, bowls, plates, etc, is usually impossible." ET-related social isolation and depression are flagged as a *secondary* impairment that affects creative flow in its own right.

### 5.4 Lederman 2007 — career impact quantification

Lederman (2007; https://doi.org/10.21091/mppa.2007.2105) studied 46 instrumental musicians with tremor. Among 26 with ET, all had hand tremor; 13 used medication as needed, 1 no longer played, 4 were lost to follow-up. Among 4 with PD, all had hand tremor and impaired dexterity interfering with playing; one stopped playing and 2 continued with medication. The study concludes: "Tremor can have a major impact on instrumental performance. Accurate identification of tremor type is critical for effective management and career counseling."

### 5.5 Parkinson's piano MIDI study

A study using MIDI technology to assess fine motor skills in Parkinson's patients (https://doi.org/10.1055/s-2007-976459) tested 25 PD patients and 31 healthy controls on an electronic piano (Yamaha CLP 110), measuring frequency (F), velocity (V), duration (DUR), inter-onset interval (IOI), and inter-stimulus interval (ISI) for each key. Results showed reduced striking frequency and duration in PD patients for all tasks except the sequence task, and significantly reduced striking velocity for single tapping and finger jumps. A landmark DBS case (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4174744/) examined a non-professional pianist with severe PD treated with subthalamic DBS. With DBS OFF, "the timing fluctuations of the performance exhibited random correlations." With DBS ON, "DBS restored long-range dependency in the temporal fluctuations, corresponding with the general motor improvement on DBS." This demonstrates that motor skill characteristics in musical performance are directly modulable by neurological intervention — and by extension that interface-level adaptations could similarly alter performance quality.

### 5.6 NIME / ADMI case studies

- **Netychords** (Davanzo, Avanzini, Ludovico; https://avanzini.di.unimi.it/downloads/publications/davanzo_chira23.pdf) reports a child with cerebral palsy who, working with this ADMI, "achieved a significant milestone, namely the enrollment in Portugal's Arts Education Program." One of the few longitudinal cases of re-entry into music-making via an adaptive interface.
- **DuoRhythmo** (CHI 2023; http://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3544548.3581285), evaluated with n=5 ALS participants, reports an **average System Usability Scale (SUS) score of 79.5** and qualitative descriptors "fun, empowering, accessible, easy to use, engaging, and stimulating." SUS > 68 is conventionally "above average," but this is eye-tracking, not tremor.
- A gaze-driven xylophone interface (https://exa.ai/library/publication/wdb1cwxbwld) reports SUS items with mean Likert ratings in the 1.7–4.0 range on a 5-point scale (n=9).
- **DexPlay** (Berkeley AHD 2023; https://edg.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/AHD-2023-group9.pdf) is a passive wrist dampener designed after a case-study interview with an ET guitarist who had given up guitar. It targets the flexion-extension wrist axis specifically, illustrating the principle of anatomically targeted intervention.
- **Ayre** (QuackHacks 2026 hackathon; https://github.com/0xrpheus/ayre) explicitly includes a "Tremor smoothing" slider on a webcam-tracked hand controller; documented as an accessibility feature, not a research study.

### 5.7 Smart-pen analogue — Kalman Filter wins on convergence

The 2025 *Scientific Reports* paper on adaptive tremor-suppression for a smart pen (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-14196-5) compares Fx-LMS, Fx-NLMS, Fx-LMS/NLMS hybrid, RLS, and Kalman filtering on real PD signals from the NewHandPD dataset. They report that RLS achieves the lowest mean squared error, but the Kalman Filter converges approximately eight times faster — relevant because convergence speed translates directly to user-perceived latency during composition.

## 6. False positive rates in gesture rejection algorithms

### 6.1 Digiball study (2025) — direct quantification

Costa's 2025 Digiball thesis (https://repositorio-aberto.up.pt/bitstream/10216/168796/2/735438.pdf) provides the most directly relevant data on false positives in accessible music gesture recognition. Using DTW and Protractor3D algorithms: with **3 training templates**, "False positives occurred when unrelated movements triggered gesture recognition, while false negatives arose due to the high variability between training samples and test gestures." With **5 training templates**, "No false positives were observed, demonstrating improved specificity. However, the system showed a higher rate of false negatives, leading to many missed recognitions." The thesis notes: "This trade-off between reducing false positives and increasing false negatives mirrors challenges discussed in Chapters 2 and 3." This finding directly illustrates the fundamental tension in tremor filtering: aggressive filtering eliminates tremor false positives but introduces performance false negatives (missed intentional gestures).

### 6.2 Netz Mixed Reality Instrument (2023)

Graf & Barthet (https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3611659.3617210) developed Netz through a three-month participatory design process with a professional keyboard player. The system uses "artificial intelligence for reducing errors in gesture interpretation" in hand-tracked mixed reality. Results showed "a deep learning model based on interactive machine learning can significantly reduce the number of technological errors in a set of musical performance tasks," identifying the direct relationship between "sensing-based technological faults and accurate control of musical expression."

### 6.3 MAGIC Summoning (2013)

Kohlsdorf et al. (https://jmlr.org/papers/volume14/kohlsdorf13a/kohlsdorf13a.pdf) developed a tool to automatically suggest gestures with low false positive probability by comparing proposed gestures against an "Everyday Gesture Library" using Symbolic Aggregate approXimation (SAX). The system can "estimate how accurately that gesture can be recognized and estimates its false positive rate by comparing it against the natural movements in the EGL" — directly applicable to designing musical gestures that are distinguishable from pathological tremor.

### 6.4 Bi-level thresholding in HCI

ACM CHI research on false positives vs. false negatives (https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3472749.3474735) establishes that "while false positive errors are often considered worse than false negative errors, it is easy to imagine situations where a false negative error has a high cost (e.g., the user is playing a fast-paced game)." For musicians, a missed note (false negative from over-aggressive tremor filtering) may be more damaging to performance than an unintended velocity spike (false positive). The paper proposes **bi-level thresholding**: "a restrictive threshold is used for initial attempts at performing a gesture, to cut down on false positive errors, coupled with a more permissive threshold following 'near misses.'"

### 6.5 The threshold trade-off in SteadyMouse

SteadyMouse's manual documents the trade-off space empirically: at 95% filter strength "the mouse will feel like it's in molasses but should at least be smooth." Reducing by ~10–20 percentage points introduces some tremor leakage in exchange for responsiveness (https://www.steadymouse.com/manual/). This mirrors the VKM finding that variability-driven inflation of thresholds is necessary in performance contexts.

## 7. Creative flow: what the literature actually says

The flow-state literature (Csikszentmihalyi's nine-dimensional construct; reproduced verbatim in https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3837225/) lists the necessary conditions for flow: challenge-skill balance, action-awareness merging, clear goals, unambiguous feedback, concentration, sense of control, loss of self-consciousness, time transformation, and autotelic experience. A Drexel Creativity Research Lab fMRI/EEG study of 32 jazz guitarists (https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/brain-scans-of-jazz-musicians-reveal-how-to-reach-a-creative-flow-state/; https://mesplaisirs.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/1-s2.0-S0028393224000393-main.pdf) found that **higher-domain-experience performers enter flow through release of conscious control**, not hyperfocus — i.e., once a motor program is well-learned, *letting go* of micro-corrections enables flow. **This is the central tension for any tremor-filtering system.** A system that demands the user micro-manage thresholds, or that introduces perceptible lag and forces compensation, fights directly against the action-awareness merging and sense of control necessary for flow.

Research on digital artists with upper limb motor impairments (Cossovich et al., 2026; https://doi.org/10.1145/3731459.3773320) found that artists "prioritized authorship and control, rejecting automated 'fixes' that, in one participant's words, 'don't feel like mine.'" The paper uses the concepts of "crip time" and "flow" to interpret results, finding that artists "manage to keep a balance between their creative immersion and physical discomfort." A companion study (https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3663548.3675654) explicitly connects flow to accessibility: "Artists often describe flow as a state of deep concentration and calm, which they identify as essential to their creative endeavours." The study found that accessibility challenges create interruptions: "the required focus required for the inspiration and flow during the artistic processes, is disrupted by the interruptions the accessibility challenges artists with motor impairments find." For musicians with tremor, a gesture rejection algorithm that misclassifies intentional performance gestures as tremor creates precisely this kind of interruption. Each false negative — each rejected note — breaks the performer's flow state.

SteadyMouse's documentation describes a notable psychological phenomenon: "once the settings are fine tuned, the restoration of control breaks a psychological feedback loop and customers find their hand tremor lessened while using SteadyMouse. Knowing that the tremor cannot get through provides a sense of relief that changes the nature of the interaction in a significant way" (https://www.steadymouse.com/purchase/). This suggests that effective filtering may itself reduce tremor severity through reduced anxiety — consistent with the known exacerbation of tremor by performance anxiety.

Quantitative link between tremor symptoms and flow disruption is not in the published HCI literature. What is documented is the existence of **biopsychosocial cascades**: ET patients document social withdrawal, anxiety in performance contexts, and depression (https://tracscotland.org/blog/essential-tremor-a-musicians-perspective-by-valerie-bryan/) — each of which independently erodes flow prerequisite states. Samuel Smith's reported 50–150-attempt/demo workflow is a flow-destroying loop by construction, even though it solves the symptom enough to finish an album.

### 7.1 What affects the variable the user can actually tune — sensitivity threshold

Although no peer-reviewed study isolates threshold sensitivity for musicians with tremor, two indirect streams exist:

1. **VKM (CHI 2022)** reports quantitatively how threshold tightening trades false positives vs. false negatives as a function of training-set size and gesture-production variability (https://cs.ucf.edu/~jjl/pubs/Taranta2022.pdf). With a single training sample, the threshold must be loose to compensate; with dense data, it can be tight without losing gestures. Implication: a per-user calibration phase of even 20–30 demonstration gestures could allow substantially tighter thresholds than the "Aggressive / Balanced / Light" taxonomies commercial tools use.
2. **SteadyMouse's manual** documents the trade-off space empirically (see §6.5).

No published study reports composition completion times as a function of filter sensitivity, but anecdotally AI-mediated workflows (Smith's 50–150 attempts) and adaptive-instrument workflows (Netychords' multi-year adaptive redesign over many sessions) suggest **multiple-orders-of-magnitude overheads for naive approaches** vs. well-tuned pipelines.

## 8. Sensitivity threshold calibration: completion times and user satisfaction

### 8.1 Quantitative data from accessible DMI studies

- The 2025 gesture-based DMI study (https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3750069.3750438) found the 73% error reduction / 22% time-per-note decrease over four sessions noted above.
- The **DuoRhythmo** CADMI for people with ALS achieved SUS 79.5 (https://www.academia.edu/124645343/; http://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3544548.3581285). Participants reported feeling "empowered and engaged, indicating significant mental stimulation and emotional relief during usage."
- An inclusive MIDI controller observational study (https://air.unimi.it/retrieve/5ca205b8-d109-44ef-afd5-9e5aef69f7a5/phd_unimi_R13911_4.pdf) used SUS scores and qualitative Think-Aloud protocols across 10 standardized tasks. One participant (P3) "reported a score of 2 for the ease of use and a score of 3 for the fun level" and "expressed a frustration level of 2 in understanding the software and a frustration level of 3 in using the software."

### 8.2 The SUPPLE++ system

Gajos et al. (2008; https://doi.org/10.1145/1357054.1357250) demonstrated that automatically-generated, ability-based interfaces improved performance for motor-impaired users: "participants with motor impairments were **26.4% faster** using ability-based user interfaces generated by SUPPLE++. They also made **73% fewer errors**, strongly preferred those interfaces to the manufacturers' defaults, and found them more efficient, easier to use, and much less physically tiring." This establishes that adaptive threshold calibration directly impacts both speed and satisfaction.

### 8.3 The Accessibility and Dimensionality Study

Research with digital musicians with quadriplegic cerebral palsy (https://nime.org/proceedings/2015/nime2015_250.pdf) found that standard X-Y control surfaces "afford discretised control over single sound events or single-destination continuous parameters." The researchers developed a multi-dimensional mapping strategy that quantified participants' gestural capabilities first, then designed interfaces to match — demonstrating that calibration to individual motor profiles enables creative expression that rigid interfaces cannot.

## 9. Motor skill retention: adaptive vs. standard interface transitions

The strongest longitudinal evidence comes from outside the DAW literature but is directly applicable:

- The **Cymis** nursing-home study (https://exa.ai/library/publication/wb8qdd8w23g) tracked 31 disabled clients playing a score-programmed electronic instrument for an average of **5.6 years** (some up to 7 years). Of those 31: **13 (42%)** showed measurable upper-limb motor progress, **17 (55%)** showed no change (5 of whom initially progressed then regressed), and **1 (3%)** deteriorated. This is direct evidence that adaptive musical interfaces can **support motor retention over multi-year horizons**, contrary to the assumption that assistive tools cause atrophy.
- Stage-specific task-specific bowing tremor is itself evidence that motor systems retain highly specific trained programs decades into disease — the violinist in PMC4117185 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4117185/) developed a *new* task-specific tremor post-lobectomy only when *playing*, not during unrelated arm use, demonstrating that pathological and trained motor programs are dissociable at the neurological level. This is consistent with the design principle that adaptive systems should target *only* the tremor-bearing signal dimension, not the learned intentional dimension.
- The Body-Machine Interface (BMI) paradigm (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4350775/; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3534847/) establishes that "the interface is subject to two processes of learning: while users practice controlling the assistive device, the interface modifies itself based on the user's residual abilities and preferences."
- Research on cerebral palsy and virtual reality interfaces (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12984-020-00689-z) found that "individuals from both groups were able to improve task performance and retain acquired information." Crucially, "the CP group presented better performance in the abstract interface than in the concrete interface, whereas, in the control group, the opposite occurred." The authors caution that "the possibility to transfer performance improvement from a VR task to a real task should be carefully considered."
- Research on transfer of mode switching in prosthesis use (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8141154/) found that "roughly 50% of able-bodied participants significantly improved their switching performance after training a short timeframe of 10 min," but notes challenges in transferring trained motor skills when interface characteristics change.

**No published study directly tracks motor-skill loss or gain when a professional musician with movement disorder toggles between a tremor-filtered interface and a standard one (e.g., turning SteadyMouse off). This remains an open empirical question.**

---

## 10. Synthesis: where the evidence stands

| Claim in brief | Evidence status |
|---|---|
| Ableton Live has "MIDI velocity smoothing" | True only in the sense that the Velocity MIDI effect supports Gate/Clip/Random modes; it is a memoryless per-note remap, not a temporal smoother (https://www.ableton.com/en/live-manual/12/live-midi-effect-reference/) |
| Ableton Live markets this for tremor | False — forum users adopt it as a workaround (https://forum.ableton.com/viewtopic.php?t=120139); no productization |
| Logic Pro's Smart Controls include tremor compensation | False — not in any official Apple documentation (https://support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/smart-controls-overview-lgcp7e59f24b/mac; https://support.apple.com/content/dam/edam/applecare/images/en_US/otherassets/accessibility/vpat_logic_pro_2024.pdf) |
| SteadyMouse is a tremor-aware cursor tool | True, extensively documented (https://www.steadymouse.com/manual/) |
| SteadyMouse distinguishes vibrato from tremor | False — operates at the OS cursor layer; no musical semantics |
| Pathological tremor is 4–12 Hz and separable from vibrato by frequency | Partly true (tremor band overlaps 3–15 Hz), but separation must exploit regularity and shape, not rate alone (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4053556/; https://pubs.aip.org/asa/jasa/article/130/1/EL1/907816/Vibrato-and-tremor-extent-spectrum-Algorithm-and) |
| Gesture rejection in HCI has been characterized with false-positive rates | True — VKM/CHI 2022 is the canonical reference (https://cs.ucf.edu/~jjl/pubs/Taranta2022.pdf); false positives are documented as more harmful than false negatives |
| Composition completion times vary with tremor-filter sensitivity | **Not documented in any peer-reviewed source accessed** |
| User satisfaction scores vary with sensitivity | Indirectly: SUS scores exist for ADMIs (DuoRhythmo SUS 79.5 — n=5 ALS; xylophone interface 1.7–4.0 Likert — n=9) but not against tremor thresholds |
| Motor skill retention changes when switching adaptive ↔ standard | **Not documented in any peer-reviewed source accessed**; closest analogue is the multi-year Cymis study (https://exa.ai/library/publication/wb8qdd8w23g) |

The most consistent finding across all examined sources is that **the asymmetry between latency and tremor-cancellation frequency matters more than raw filter strength** — and the only settings a current commercial or research tool exposes to a user to control it are coarse sliders (SteadyMouse) or coarse MIDI gates (Ableton's Velocity MIDI effect). The HCI literature has demonstrated (VKM; Kalman smart pen; STFT tremor switch; WFLC; E-BMFLC) that finer-grained rejection is achievable in principle, including preserving intentional motion through tremor — but has not crossed over into DAW-level real-time MIDI pipelines.

What the literature has not yet produced, and what an honest reading of the evidence suggests is missing, is a longitudinal, randomized comparison of composition completion time and flow-state metrics across (a) no-filter, (b) cursor-level filter (SteadyMouse), and (c) MIDI-semantic filter conditions for professional musicians with movement disorders. The infrastructure for such a study exists — the SUS instruments, the Flow State Scale (Martin & Jackson, 2008), and the VKM-style rejection framework — but the application to expressive musical input remains future work.

---

## 11. Research gaps and recommendations

1. **No published study directly measures the impact of MIDI tremor filtering on DAW composition workflows.** WFLC has been validated for pen input and joystick control but never tested with MIDI keyboard performance data.
2. **No DAW vendor has published tremor-specific input processing research.** This represents a significant opportunity for both Ableton and Apple/Logic Pro.
3. **The false positive/negative trade-off in musical gesture recognition has not been quantified for pathological tremor populations.** The Digiball study provides the closest data but used participants with intellectual/developmental disabilities, not motor tremor.
4. **No study has measured composition completion times or SUS scores for musicians with tremor using DAW-specific adaptive interfaces.** Existing SUS data (DuoRhythmo: 79.5) comes from different contexts.
5. **Longitudinal studies of motor skill retention when switching between tremor-filtered and standard MIDI interfaces are absent from the literature.**
6. **The vibrato/tremor discrimination problem in real-time MIDI capture remains fundamentally unsolved** and represents a high-value research target at the intersection of HCI, signal processing, and music technology.
7. **No data on the latency budget of MIDI anti-tremor filtering in DAW contexts or perceptual thresholds (e.g., 10–20 ms)** relevant to real-time performance.
8. **No systematic survey of MIDI controller hardware with built-in anti-tremor firmware** (accessible MIDI controllers in the NIME/ADMI space), which would be the most direct production solutions.
9. **No treatment of the role of audio quantization, post-hoc MIDI editing, or offline correction workflows** as alternative "non-real-time" tremor accommodations for composition vs. performance tasks.
10. **No treatment of how orchestral/ensemble synchronization, tempo tracking, or click-track interaction would be affected** by tremor-induced latency variation in adaptive filtering.

The strongest single new study to fill the literature gap would be a randomized comparison of no-filter vs. cursor-level filter vs. MIDI-semantic filter conditions measuring completion time, SUS, and Flow State Scale in musicians with ET/PD. Any practical deployment requires (a) accepting frequency-only separation is impossible, (b) building regularity/context features, (c) per-user calibration, (d) latency budgets below ~10–20 ms, and (e) flow-state-friendly design that avoids demanding user micro-management of thresholds — paralleling the VKM finding that tighter thresholds require denser training samples.

# Cyber Insurance Comparison: Chubb vs. Coalition vs. Cowbell Cyber
## 15-Employee Austin, TX Business · $2–5M Revenue · Dual PCI-DSS/HIPAA Exposure

---

## Bottom Line Up Front

**Coalition** offers the strongest technical fit for dual PCI/HIPAA exposure: its published matrix lists **PCI Fines & Assessments and Regulatory Defense & Penalties at "no sublimit"** (full policy limit), with an **express contractual-liability carveback** for the PCI section that directly addresses the *P.F. Chang's v. Federal Insurance* denial fact pattern (https://www.itpaystobecovered.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/15/2017/02/PF_Chang_v_Fed_Ins.pdf). **Chubb** offers the broadest wording, a healthcare-specific product (up to $20M, Consumer Redress at full limits, 100% defense allocation) (https://www.chubb.com/us-en/business-insurance/chubb-privacy-protection-for-healthcare-managed-care-organizations.html), and the most granular response SLA, but Regulatory Fines/Payment Card Loss are scheduled sublimits and a **Neglected Software Exploit coinsurance escalates 0%→50% based on patch latency** (https://www.chubb.com/content/dam/chubb-sites/chubb-com/au-en/business/cyber-insurance/documents/pdf/chubb10_571_0722_cyber_enterprise_risk_management.pdf). **Cowbell** is the fastest to quote (sub-5-minute AI underwriting) but its Prime 100 has an API-level override **capping limits at $2M for revenue under $5M** and $500K–$1M sublimits for PCI/Regulatory in small-limit examples (https://developers.cowbellcyber.ai/reference/requesting-a-p100-quote; https://meetings.boardbook.org/Documents/DownloadPDF/e2bb4bf7-190d-400a-abf1-b242477fbe0c?org=1303).

---

## 1. Regulatory Fine Coverage and How Sublimits Work

### The Trap: PCI Assessments Are Contractual, Not Regulatory

Card-brand assessments flow from your Merchant Services Agreement, not from a statute. In *P.F. Chang's v. Federal Insurance* (an Ace/Chubb subsidiary), the court upheld denial of ~$1.9M in assessments under a "liability assumed by any Insured under any contract or agreement" exclusion (https://www.theclm.org/Magazine/articles/a-matter-of-interpretation-cyber/1752). A policy that covers only "regulatory fines insurable by law" may not respond to PCI assessments at all. Verify an affirmative PCI endorsement with the contractual-liability exclusion carved back.

**Coalition carves back the contractual-liability exclusion specifically for the PCI section** — its comparison sheet lists "Contractual Liability — Yes, carvebacks for: (1) Section Network and Information Security Liability …; (3) Section PCI Fines and Assessments" (https://insurancemastersinc.com/__static/jdj5jdewjhvzn3e0rfrjclphdkzqt2nj/Cyber-Coalition_Coverages_RPS.pdf). This is the single most consequential differentiator for a card-accepting business.

### Sublimit Mechanics Across All Three

A sublimit is a cap *within, not in addition to,* your aggregate. A $1M aggregate with a $500K PCI sublimit gives you $1M total with only $500K available for PCI fines/assessments — and defense costs typically erode that same sublimit (Cowbell's form states: "AMOUNTS INCURRED AS DEFENSE EXPENSE UNDER THIS POLICY WILL REDUCE AND MAY EXHAUST THE LIMIT OF LIABILITY" — https://home.sayatalabs.com/cnc-wb/get_resource/carriers/SAMPLE_POLICY_FORM/COWBELL). Standard market practice; verify whether defense sits inside or outside the sublimit on your declarations page.

### Carrier-by-Carrier Structure

| Carrier | PCI Coverage Architecture | Regulatory/HIPAA Architecture | Sublimit Reality |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Chubb Cyber ERM** | "Payment Card Loss" sublimit (Consumer Redress Fund and Payment Card Loss each ~20% of aggregate per specimen forms) (https://lmalloyds.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Chubb-Cyber-ERM-Policy-US-1.pdf) | "Regulatory Proceedings / Regulatory Fines" sublimit; Consumer Redress also sublimited | Scheduled, add-on sublimits purchased via the declarations page. Chubb's healthcare product puts Consumer Redress at **full limits** (not sublimited) |
| **Coalition** | "PCI Fines & Assessments" — separate insuring agreement, **"no sublimit"** in published matrix | "Regulatory Actions" full policy limit | Full-aggregate treatment on the most consequential coverages for this profile |
| **Cowbell Prime 100** | "PCI Fines & Penalties" — scheduled third-party sublimit; example docs show $500K–$1M at small limits (https://img1.wsimg.com/blobby/go/df823d3e-ce95-46ad-a9ac-0ec5ee299bdf/FLY-CB-5CN3LZ4ZP_Certificate.pdf) | "Regulator Defense & Penalties" — similarly sublimited ($500K–$1M in examples) | Smallest sublimit headroom of the three for the buyer's profile |

### "Insurable by Law" — The Real Gate

All three pay fines only "to the extent insurable by applicable law." HIPAA civil monetary penalties are generally uninsurable as a matter of public policy in most states, but defense costs are covered. Three FCC mechanism matters here:

- **Most Favored Venue language**: Cowbell's Liability Costs definition covers punitive/exemplary damages "but only to the extent such damages are insurable under the applicable law most favorable to the insurability of such damages" (https://developers.cowbellcyber.ai/reference/coverage-definitions). Chubb's guide similarly lists "Most favored jurisdiction applicability to punitive, exemplary, and multiplied damages." This clause — by referencing whichever connected jurisdiction is most favorable — is what makes GDPR/CCPA/HIPAA-adjacent penalties collectible.
- **Punitive vs. compensatory**: Compensatory fines are typically insurable; punitive fines typically are not (https://seedpodcyber.com/does-cyber-insurance-cover-regulatory-fines/).
- **Stacking exposure**: With HIPAA Tier 1 minimums at **$145/violation** and a maximum annual cap of **$2,190,294** per identical provision (2025 inflation-adjusted — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-45/subtitle-A/subchapter-A/part-102; https://www.hipaajournal.com/2024-civil-monetary-penalties-hipaa-violations/), and OCR's enforcement discretion lowering effective Tier 1–3 caps to ~$36,505/$146,053/$365,052, exposure is per-violation and stacks quickly when multiple Security Rule provisions fail together.

### Texas-Specific Exposure Layered On Top

- **TDPSA (effective July 1, 2024)**: Texas AG-exclusive enforcement, 30-day cure period, then civil penalties up to **$7,500 per violation** (https://www.oag.state.tx.us/consumer-protection/file-consumer-complaint/consumer-privacy-rights/texas-data-privacy-and-security-act). No private right of action. A breach affecting 5,000 Texans has a theoretical TDPSA ceiling of 5,000 × $7,500 = **$37.5M** — far above any SMB policy limit.
- **Texas Identity Theft Enforcement and Protection Act**: 60-day individual notice window, AG notice **tightened to 30 days** (effective Sept 1, 2023) for breaches affecting ≥250 Texans via the OAG electronic form (https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/consumer-protection/data-breach-reporting; https://www.mintz.com/insights-center/viewpoints/2826/2023-07-07-texas-has-been-busy-ramping-up-privacy-protections-new).
- **Card-brand penalties**: Monthly escalation from $5,000–$10,000 initially to $100,000/month for sustained non-compliance (https://www.bloccyber.com/retail-cyber-insurance/texas).

---

## 2. Incident Response Services and SLAs

| Carrier | First Touch | Subsequent Steps | IR Model | Notable Economics |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Chubb** | "Matter of minutes" via Chubb Cyber Alert® app; 800-817-2665 (https://www.chubb.com/us-en/business-insurance/products/cyber-insurance/cyber-incident-response-solutions.html). Chubb's 1-min/1-hour ladder appears on UK/AU pages (https://www.chubb.com/uk-en/business/products/cyber-erm/cyber-incident-response-process-.html); US incident-response communications describe mobilization "within 24 hours upon your instruction" | IR Coach (outside attorney) coordinates panel vendors | External panel (pre-negotiated rates; not required) | Emergency IR Expenses (first 48 hrs) at **$0 retention** for SME/middle market (https://www.chubb.com/content/dam/chubb-sites/chubb-com/au-en/business/cyber-insurance/documents/pdf/cyber-erm-version-2-2-policy-sme-marketplace-platform-au.pdf). Complimentary "Cyber Stack" (vulnerability outreach, training, dedicated Cyber Risk Advisor) free for businesses under 100 employees (https://www.chubb.com/content/dam/chubb-sites/chubb-com/us-en/business-insurance/products/cyber/documents/chubb_cyber_appetiteguide.pdf) |
| **Coalition** | **5 minutes average** documented (https://assets.ctfassets.net/rtv7ooun71u4/2NyUB0Rya6LPoVMir1TPgR/d3ba214e13a2b880b39208afd422c61f/Coalition_Partner-Datasheet_SentinelOne) | Immediate CIR engagement, 2-hour panel legal consultation free | In-house CIR affiliate (wholly owned, not third-party panel) | **$0 out-of-pocket retention** for security/forensics when using CIR (https://www.coalitioninc.com/announcements/coalition-eliminates-out-of-pocket-security-and-forensics-costs-for-policyholders-facing-a-cyber-claim). 45% of incidents resolved with no claim opened/no cost; 84% stolen-funds recovery rate |
| **Cowbell** | **1-hour initial acknowledgement** (https://cowbell.insure/claims-services/); 833-633-8666 | Immediate scoping call, panel dispatch | In-house claims + curated vendor panel (CyberClan guarantees 15-min IR response / 1-hour SOW) | 65% ransom-demand reduction. Cowbell Resiliency Services (Feb 2025 launch) provides SpearTip-backed 24/7/365 U.S. SOC; deductible waiver on Breach Fund available when MDR deployed across all endpoints (https://cowbell.insure/news-events/pr/crs-launch/) |

**Coalition's 5-minute number is operational, not a contractual SLA guarantee**; Chubb and Cowbell publish operational metrics similarly without contractual guarantees. **Coalition's in-house CIR affiliate is the structurally distinctive model** — it negotiates with threat actors directly and reduces vendor-coordination friction during the worst hour of an incident.

### Pre-Breach Tools (Material Differentiator)

- **Coalition Control**: free active monitoring for all policyholders — exposed assets, unpatched vulns, compromised credentials. Coalition reports **73% fewer claims** among engaged policyholders (https://playciso.com/blog/cyber-insurance-comparison-carriers-cost-2026).
- **Chubb Cyber Stack**: complimentary for <100 employees; vulnerability outreach, training tools, dedicated Risk Advisor.
- **Cowbell Connectors + Cowbell Factors**: continuous risk scoring that rewards improving posture at renewal.

---

## 3. Credit Monitoring and Legal Defense

### Credit Monitoring

- **Chubb**: Included in Data Breach Fund. On the Healthcare form, "Credit monitoring expenses (no longer tied to privacy regulations)" — coverage applies regardless of whether state law mandates it (https://www.chubb.com/content/dam/chubb-sites/chubb-com/us-en/cyber-risk-management/agent-center/pdfs/2020-06.23-14-01-1295-commercial-cyber-policy-guide-for-agents-brokers.pdf). The Chubb commercial cyber guide states credit monitoring applies "without a limitation of time (no cap of 12 or 24 months)."
- **Coalition**: Included in Breach Response Costs. "No cap. Up to 1 year or longer if required by law."
- **Cowbell**: Security Breach Expense explicitly includes "Credit/Identity Monitoring Expenses: … for a period of up to one year (or more if required by law)" (https://home.sayatalabs.com/cnc-wb/get_resource/carriers/SAMPLE_POLICY_FORM/COWBELL). Breach Fund also includes "healthcare records remediation" — a tangible differentiator for your profile.

### Legal Defense

| Dimension | Chubb | Coalition | Cowbell |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Defense cost treatment** | Within limits (consumption) | Within limits | Within limits; explicitly "REDUCE AND MAY EXHAUST THE LIMIT OF LIABILITY" |
| **Trigger basis** | **Claims-Made** (more favorable than "Claims-Made and Reported") (https://www.chubb.com/content/dam/chubb-sites/chubb-com/us-en/cyber-risk-management/agent-center/pdfs/2020-06.23-14-01-1295-commercial-cyber-policy-guide-for-agents-brokers.pdf) | **Claims-Made and Reported** | **Claims-Made and Reported** |
| **Allocation provision** | **Healthcare form: affirmative 100% allocation of defense** if at least one covered claim asserted (https://www.chubb.com/us-en/business-insurance/chubb-privacy-protection-for-healthcare-managed-care-organizations.html) | Standard | Standard |
| **Hammer clause** | 80/20 hammer language | Not publicly specified | 50% hammer on withheld-consent settlements (https://home.sayatalabs.com/cnc-wb/get_resource/carriers/SAMPLE_POLICY_FORM/COWBELL) |
| **Defense for HIPAA OCR investigation** | Cyber ERM covers; Healthcare Privacy form purpose-built for this | Covered under Regulatory Actions | Covered under Regulatory Defense & Penalties within Security Breach Liability |
| **Defense for PCI proceedings** | Covered under Payment Card Loss | Covered under separate PCI Fines & Assessments agreement | Covered within Security Breach Liability |

Chubb's healthcare-specific **100% defense allocation** is materially broader than standard cyber market practice — preventing the insurer from allocating defense costs between covered and uncovered claims.

---

## 4. Policy Exclusions Relevant to E-Commerce

### Universal Across All Three

1. **War / nation-state** — all use 2024 Lloyd's market wording (LMA5564 family, mandatory since March 31, 2023 — https://www.insurancejournal.com/news/national/2023/04/04/715079.htm). Post-Merck v. Ace American, carriers are structurally more likely to deny on attribution-disputed claims. Critical implication: Coalition/Cowbell/Chubb may deny coverage for e-skimming campaigns attributed to nation-state actors.
2. **Bodily injury / property damage** — Cowbell's form excludes mental anguish except where caused by Security Breach/Cyber Incident/Extortion Threat.
3. **Prior known acts** — Coalition warns explicitly on its application that undisclosed known circumstances void the underlying claim (https://landy.com/apps/cyber/Coalition-Cyber-USA-NEWAPP-COMBINED-202302.pdf).
4. **Unencrypted devices** — disclosure-required on Coalition application; lack of encryption is treated as a material representation, not a surcharge item.
5. **Power failure / infrastructure** — Cowbell excludes "failure of, reduction in, or surge of power, regardless of the cause."

### E-Commerce-Specific Gotchas

| Gotcha | Why It Matters for You |
|---|---|
| **Contractual liability for PCI fines** | Card-brand fines flow from the Merchant Services Agreement. The P.F. Chang's case shows how this exclusion can defeat coverage. **Verify an affirmative PCI endorsement with the contractual-liability exclusion carved back** — Coalition does this expressly; Chubb/Cowbell do so via their PCI insuring agreements |
| **Ransomware sublimit** | Category default 25–50% of headline limit per market analysis (https://www.sideguysolutions.com/shareables/cyber-insurance-coverage-inclusions-exclusions-war-ransomware-social-engineering-nation-state-2026.html). A $1M policy may carry a $250K–$500K ransom sublimit. Coalition: typically 50%, up to 100% endorsement; Chubb: 25–50%; Cowbell: SMB category default, $500K–$1M API-defined |
| **Social engineering / BEC** | Carved out of main coverage on most policies; $250K–$1M sublimits typically. Cowbell's Impersonation Fraud is **only on Prime 100 Pro and Prime 250**, not base Prime 100 (https://cowbell.insure/wp-content/uploads/pdfs/CB-CyberProductComparisonPrime100vsPrime250vsPrimePro.pdf). Coalition: $250K–$1M depending on policy size |
| **Cyber-physical / IoT** | Standard exclusion; SMB endorsement typically $5K–$25K extra. For POS-connected infrastructure, ask explicitly |
| **Reputation / brand recovery** | Structurally **not covered** across all three despite marketing. Long-tail brand damage falls outside every policy form |
| **Unsupported software** | Emerging market-wide exclusion; Chubb's Neglected Software Exploit coinsurance (0% at 0–45 days; 5% at 46–90; 10% at 91–180; 25% at 181–365; **50% beyond 365 days**) creates a coverage haircut for slow patching on CMS/plugin stacks typical of SMB e-commerce (https://www.chubb.com/content/dam/chubb-sites/chubb-com/au-en/business/cyber-insurance/documents/pdf/chubb10_571_0722_cyber_enterprise_risk_management.pdf) |
| **BIPA** | Cowbell Prime 250 has a mandatory BIPA exclusion; Prime One offers BIPA coverage as option (https://cowbell.insure/wp-content/uploads/pdfs/CB-CyberProductComparisonPrimeOnevsPrime250.pdf). Material only if you deploy biometric login |
| **Pixel/wrongful collection** | Cowbell Prime 250/One offer Wrongful Collection coverage; market-wide emerging exclusion for tracking pixels/session replay on e-commerce sites |

### PCI DSS 4.0.1 (Mandatory March 31, 2025) — Direct Underwriting Hook

The 64 new requirements, 51 future-dated, became mandatory **March 31, 2025**. Notable for e-commerce:

- **Req. 6.4.3**: payment-page script authorization, integrity verification, written inventory
- **Req. 11.6.1**: change/tamper detection on payment pages, at least weekly (aimed at e-skimming — https://blog.pcisecuritystandards.org/new-information-supplement-payment-page-security-and-preventing-e-skimming; https://www.securitymetrics.com/program-education/pci-dss-v4-ecommerce-faqs)
- **SAQ A eligibility** clarified for merchants fully outsourcing via iframe/redirect

Non-compliance is both a fine/assessment risk and an underwriting red flag — carriers now ask what PCI DSS level you're at (Level 1–4 or "Not Compliant"; Chubb's application is explicit on this — https://www.chubb.com/content/dam/chubb-sites/chubb-com/ie-en/business/by-category-cyber/11374b-chubb_cyber_erm_extensive_proposal_form_ie_update.pdf).

### 4a. Coalition Active Cyber Policy (April 15, 2025 Material Update)

As of April 15, 2025, US non-admitted new and renewal business moved to the **Active Cyber Policy**: full-policy-limit reset for each separate first-party incident ("unlimited reinstatements" for eligible businesses), expanded privacy liability beyond the insured's own privacy policy, affirmative **betterment costs**, optional separate limit for Breach Response (preserves main limits), AI/deepfake coverage, SEC disclosure cost coverage. Limits **up to $15M** and revenue up to $5B (https://www.coalitioninc.com/blog/cyber-insurance/introducing-the-active-cyber-policy; https://help.coalitioninc.com/hc/en-us/articles/33998071846811-Active-Cyber-Policy-FAQ). Pre-April-2025 comparison documents may understate Coalition's current terms.

---

## 5. Premium Factors for $2–5M / 15 Employees / Dual PCI + HIPAA

### Underwriter Model

The Insurance Curator 2024 formula (https://insurancecurator.com/how-cybersecurity-insurance-premiums-are-calculated-the-2024-formula/) weights:

| Variable | Weight | Direction |
|---|---|---|
| Industry | 25% | Healthcare/Finance high |
| Revenue | 20% | Linear escalation |
| Data sensitivity | 15% | PII/PHI multiplier |
| Security controls | 20% | Up to 40% reduction |
| Loss history | 10% | 15–150% surcharge |
| Jurisdiction | 10% | CA/NY surcharge (Texas neutral) |

**Base rate**: $400–$1,200 per $1M limit for revenue under $50M.

### Data-Type and Industry Multipliers for Your Profile

| Factor | Multiplier |
|---|---|
| Healthcare data (PHI) | 1.4× |
| Payment card (PCI) | 1.3× |
| Combined dual data factor | ~1.82× on data-sensitivity component |
| Healthcare & Life Sciences industry | 1.35× |
| Retail & Hospitality | 1.20× |

### Indicative Premium — Range of Estimates

Panel sources disagree on Cowbell positioning: some place it at parity with Coalition (~$950–$1,400) and some as most expensive (~$7,800–$8,500 for $1M). I'm flagging the disagreement rather than resolving it.

| Source | Range | Profile |
|---|---|---|
| Insureon SMB average | ~$1,552/yr ($129/mo); broad SMB range $400–$8,000 (https://www.insureon.com/small-business-insurance/cyber-liability/cost) | All SMB |
| CyberPolicyFinder | $1,000–$3,000/yr for $1M–$2M (https://cyberpolicyfinder.com/us/cyber-insurance/cost) | 11–50 emp, $10K–$25K ded |
| Canopy (Texas e-commerce) | $1,000–$5,000/yr for $1M — financial/e-commerce at the higher end (https://canopyinsurancetexas.com/cyber-insurance-texas-businesses/) | TX e-commerce |
| Insurance Curator (1M limit, $5K retention, good controls) | Coalition/Cowbell/Hiscox SMB: $950–$1,400; **Chubb: 15–25% higher** (https://insurancecurator.com/how-small-businesses-qualify-for-cybersecurity-insurance-with-limited-resources/) | SMB, well-controlled |

### Estimate for Your Profile

For a 15-employee, ~$3.5M revenue, dual PCI/HIPAA Austin business with average controls and no loss history, seeking **$1M aggregate**: roughly **$1,100–$2,500**. For **$2M aggregate**: roughly **$2,200–$5,000**. Adding higher ransomware sublimit elections typically loads **10–20%**.

### Top Premium Drivers — Ranked for Your Profile

1. **Dual PCI + HIPAA data exposure** is the dominant multiplier. Carriers will explicitly ask about both on the application.
2. **Security controls** can reduce premium **20–60%** (https://ciberinsurance.org/blog/cyber-insurance-pricing-2025/; https://insurancecurator.com/how-cybersecurity-insurance-premiums-are-calculated-the-2024-formula/):
   - MFA on email, VPN, privileged/admin accounts (now a baseline requirement, not a discount)
   - EDR on all endpoints
   - Offline, immutable, or air-gapped backups
   - Tested incident response plan
   - Documented employee security awareness training
   - **Implementation cost for 15 employees: <$1,400/year** per Insurance Curator
3. **PCI transaction volume** (Coalition bands: <100K / 100K–500K / 500K–1M / >1M) and **PCI compliance level** (1–4 or "Not Compliant") — non-compliance can result in declined quotes, sublimit reductions, or PCI exclusion endorsements.
4. **HIPAA compliance posture**: Cowbell measures HIPAA compliance directly in its Cowbell Factors risk score; failure to demonstrate (no recent risk assessment, no documented policies) materially impacts eligibility/pricing.
5. **Number of PHI/PCI records**: Coalition bands as <100K, 100K–500K, 500K–1M, >1M.
6. **Headcount of 15** puts you in the 10–19 band — the priciest sub-band for cyber because "more employees means more error. 60% of breaches involve human error" (https://www.moneygeek.com/insurance/business/cyber/cost/).
7. **Revenue ($2–5M)** is below the $50M threshold where base-rate scaling bites — data type dominates the calc.
8. **Claims history**: a prior cyber claim adds **15–150% surcharge** (https://insurancecurator.com/how-cybersecurity-insurance-premiums-are-calculated-the-2024-formula/) or 2–5× in some sources.
9. **Encryption**: increasingly a precondition, not a discount — Coalition's application treats lack of encryption as a material disclosure question.

---

| HIPAA/Regulatory | "Regulatory Fines" sublimit; **Healthcare Privacy form** puts Consumer Redress at full limits | "Regulatory Actions" full policy limit | "Regulator Defense & Penalties" sublimit |
| Defense within limits? | Yes; Cyber ERM consumption; Healthcare form: **100% allocation** of defense | Yes (Claims-Made and Reported) | Yes; explicit exhaustion language |

---

## 7. Recommendation Fit for This Profile

**Choose Coalition if:** speed-to-bind, transparency on the most consequential sublimits, and the contractual-liability carveback for PCI dominate your decision. The in-house CIR affiliate + $0 retention structure minimizes economic friction during an incident, and Coalition Control's continuous scanning reduces the prior-knowledge exclusion risk. Active Cyber Policy's unlimited reinstatements and optional separate Breach Response limit are meaningful for a 15-employee firm managing dual exposure on a $1M–$2M aggregate.

**Choose Chubb if:** you have an existing Chubb commercial relationship, anticipate global/enterprise growth, or operate in healthcare-adjacent exposure where the **Healthcare Privacy Protection product** materially broadens regulatory coverage (Consumer Redress at full limits, 100% defense allocation, uncapped credit monitoring time, up to $20M limits). Accept the 15–25% premium load versus InsurTechs and the 1-min/1-hour IR SLA documented internationally. For an e-commerce CMS/plugin stack, audit your patch SLAs against the Neglected Software Exploit coinsurance schedule.

**Choose Cowbell if:** fastest quote-to-bind and lowest overhead are the priority. The Prime 100 streamlines SMB underwriting but caps you at $2M aggregate given your revenue, and PCI/Regulatory sublimits in example docs sit below headline aggregate. Verify the actual scheduled sublimits on the quote, not example certificates.

---

## 8. Pre-Bind Action Items (Regardless of Carrier)

1. Run an external attack-surface scan and disclose all findings in the application. Undisclosed findings the carrier later discovers void the policy on the underlying claim.
2. Implement MFA on email, VPN, admin accounts. Baseline requirement, not a discount.
3. Deploy EDR on all endpoints; Cowbell may waive Breach Fund deductible if SpearTip MDR is used.
4. Document and test an incident response plan.
5. Encrypt all laptops, desktops, and portable media. Disclose encryption status accurately.
6. Verify PCI DSS compliance level (1–4) and document it. Adopt SAQ A eligibility analysis if fully outsourcing via iframe/redirect.
7. Confirm HIPAA Security Rule safeguards are in place — risk analysis, access management, audit controls, contingency planning. These are the provisions OCR most frequently cites.
8. Negotiate the ransomware sublimit up from the default 50% if budget allows — particularly relevant given 2024–2025 SMB ransomware trends and PCI DSS 4.0.1 Req. 11.6.1 tamper-detection requirements.
9. Read the exclusions endorsement (often 60+ pages) before binding. **The sublimit table is what you actually bought; the headline policy limit is marketing.**
10. Confirm Texas-specific breach-notice timing (60-day individual notice; **30-day AG notice** since Sept 1, 2023 for breaches affecting ≥250 Texans) is reflected in breach response cost coverage.
