# The Glaser–Strauss Divergence, Charmaz's Constructivist Resolution, and Contemporary Dominance in Grounded Theory

## 1. The 1967 Common Ground and Its Inbuilt Contradiction

Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss jointly published *The Discovery of Grounded Theory* in 1967 against the dominant hypothetico-deductive, grand-theory-verification paradigm of mid-century sociology. Their shared objective was to establish qualitative research as a rigorous alternative capable of generating theory from data: "We have linked this position with a general method of comparative analysis…with various procedures designed to generate grounded theory. Although our emphasis is on generating theory rather than verifying it, we take special pains not to divorce those two activities, both necessary to the scientific enterprise" (Glaser & Strauss, 1967, Preface; http://www.sxf.uevora.pt/wp-content/uploads/2013/03/Glaser_1967.pdf).

The book's disciplinary origins—Glaser's quantitative training at Columbia under Lazarsfeld and Merton, and Strauss's Chicago-school symbolic interactionism and pragmatism—"planted the seeds of divergent directions" (Charmaz, 2009, p. 129, cited in Rieger, 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6559166/). Udo Kelle's definitive reconstruction (2007) demonstrates that the 1967 text contained two *conflicting* methodological commitments: (a) a strict inductivist rhetoric that categories "emerge" from data only if the researcher ignores the literature (Glaser & Strauss 1967, p. 37: researchers should "literally ignore the literature of theory and fact on the area under study, in order to assure that the emergence of categories will not be contaminated"), and (b) an acknowledgment that "the researcher does not approach reality as a tabula rasa. He must have a perspective that will help him see relevant data" (1967, p. 3), operationalized through *theoretical sensitivity* (https://d-nb.info/1186821515/34). The methodological split was not, as sometimes claimed, a product of early estrangement; Glaser and Strauss continued to co-publish through the 1970s (*Anguish*, *Status Passage*, *Chronic Illness and the Quality of Life*). The rupture became public only after the 1990 publication of Strauss and Corbin's *Basics of Qualitative Research*—"the flagship event that marks the split" (Holton 2008, cited in https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/16094069221149486).

## 2. Glaser's *Theoretical Sensitivity* (1978): The Classic GT Position

Published eleven years after the joint text, *Theoretical Sensitivity: Advances in the Methodology of Grounded Theory* (Sociology Press, 1978; ~24,252 Google Scholar citations per https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&user=mq4fkIUAAAAJ, ~6,120 per OpenAlex https://explore.openalex.org/authors/a5044483808) was widely treated as the operational companion to the 1967 text and was used by graduate students of both Glaser and Strauss as the primary procedural guide throughout the late 1970s (Grounded Theory Review, 2009, https://groundedtheoryreview.com/2009/06/2013/). Charmaz herself called it "the most definitive early statement of the method" (http://www.sxf.uevora.pt/wp-content/uploads/2013/03/Charmaz_2006.pdf).

**Objectivist epistemology.** Glaser treated data as something "discovered" rather than constructed. He wrote that through constant comparison, "Personal input by a researcher soon drops out as eccentric and the data become objectivist not constructionist" (Glaser, 2002, p. 6, cited in Rieger, 2019). The title *The Discovery of Grounded Theory* itself encodes the assumption that an external reality exists to be found (Charmaz, 2000, https://qualquant.org/wp-content/uploads/text/Charmaz%202000.pdf). Glaser (2002) stated that CGGT "makes the generated theory as objective as humanly possible" (p. 6).

**Two-tier coding architecture.** Glaser formalized *substantive coding* (comprising open coding and selective coding, producing categories tied directly to the empirical substance of the data) and *theoretical coding*—deployed strictly *after* substantive codes have emerged—which "conceptualize how the substantive codes may relate to each other as hypotheses to be integrated into a theory" (Glaser 1978, p. 72, quoted in Kelle, https://d-nb.info/1186821515/34). He offered at least 18 "coding families"—loosely organized lists of formal and sociological terms (degree family, dimension family, cultural family, strategy family, means-goal family, the famous "Six C's," etc.) to assist this later integration phase; by 2005, the catalogue had reached 50 individual codes across 18+ families (Glaser, 1978, 1998, 2005; Hernandez, 2009, *Grounded Theory Review* 8(3):51–66, https://groundedtheoryreview.org/index.php/gtr/article/download/452/394/1204).

**Emergence as cardinal principle.** Glaser (1992): "Categories emerge upon comparison and properties emerge upon more comparison. And that is all there is to it" (quoted in Charmaz, 2000, p. 512). He warned that prior theoretical knowledge will "contaminate, be constrained by, inhibit, stifle or otherwise impede the researcher's effort to generate categories, their properties, and theoretical codes" (Glaser, 1992, quoted in Kelle, https://d-nb.info/1186821515/34).

**Delayed literature review.** Classic GT "generally prohibits preliminary literature reviews…arguing that they might affect emergence…If the researcher is aware of existent concepts, found in the literature, these might contaminate the theory, distorting its social reality" (https://uwe-repository.worktribe.com/OutputFile/6003806). Glaser argued for "reading in *unrelated* fields" while deferring substantive-area literature to the sorting stage (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grounded_theory_(Glaser); Glaser 1992, p. 35: "reading and use of literature is not forsaken in the beginning... but in unrelated fields").

**Limited role for verification.** "The goal of grounded theory is to generate a conceptual theory that accounts for a pattern of behavior which is relevant and problematic for those involved. The goal is not voluminous description, nor clever verification" (Glaser 1978, p. 93, quoted in Glaser & Holton 2004, https://groundedtheoryreview.org/index.php/gtr/article/download/94/61/343). Evaluation criteria: *fit, work, relevance, modifiability* (Glaser, 1978; Rieger, 2019, Table 3).

## 3. Strauss and Corbin's *Basics of Qualitative Research* (1990): The Straussian Counter-Reformulation

Strauss's earlier solo book, *Qualitative Analysis for Social Scientists* (1987), drew extensively from Glaser's *Theoretical Sensitivity* and was not perceived as a fundamental break (Bryant, 2009, *Forum Qualitative Sozialforschung* 10(3), https://doi.org/10.17169/fqs-10.3.1358). The rupture came with the 1990 publication of *Basics of Qualitative Research: Grounded Theory Procedures and Techniques*, co-authored with Juliet Corbin. As Strauss explained in a 1994 interview, the book was "explicitly aimed at students starting out on their research, with perhaps little or no idea about qualitative research as such" (Legewie & Schervier-Legewie, 2004, cited in Bryant, 2009). Glaser's camp later labeled the result "Full Conceptual Description" rather than genuine grounded theory (Glaser, 1992, p. 6, cited in https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?httpsredir=1&article=1085&context=dberspeakers).

**Three-stage coding architecture.** (1) *Open coding*—line-by-line or word-by-word scrutiny producing concepts; (2) *Axial coding*—"intense analysis done around one category at a time in terms of the paradigm items" (Strauss, 1987, p. 32, cited in https://www.qualitative-research.net/index.php/fqs/article/download/467/1001); (3) *Selective coding*—selecting a core category and relating all categories to it. In the third edition (Corbin & Strauss, 2008, 2015), the final stage was renamed "theoretical integration" (Rieger, 2019, Table 2).

**The coding paradigm.** A structured scaffolding of items—causal conditions, phenomenon, context, intervening conditions, action/interaction strategies, consequences—intended to make relations between codes explicit, especially during axial coding (Strauss, 1987, pp. 27–28; Strauss & Corbin, 1990). The conditional/consequential matrix extended this to macro–micro links. The paradigm was derived not from a generic list of coding families but from "one general model of action" rooted in pragmatist and interactionist social theory (Kelle, https://d-nb.info/1186821515/34).

**More permissive literature stance.** Strauss and Corbin (1990, p. 56, quoted in Kelle, https://d-nb.info/1186821515/34) announced "a more liberal position concerning the role of literature in the research process, maintaining that 'all kinds of literature can be used before a research study is begun.'" Their now-famous phrase, adopted as the slogan of the divergence, was that grounded theory requires an "open mind," not an "empty mind" (Jones & Alony 2011, cited in https://nsuworks.nova.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1416&context=tqr).

**Verification accepted.** Strauss and Corbin reversed the emphasis from the 1967 text: deduction and verification became legitimate throughout the analytic process; the conditional matrix, axial coding paradigm, and "waving the red flag" / "flip-flop" techniques are explicitly verificational tools (Strauss & Corbin, 1990; Rieger, 2019, Table 2). Evaluation criteria expanded to seven: fit, applicability, concepts, contextualization of concepts, logic, depth, integration (Corbin & Strauss, 2008, 2015; Rieger, 2019, Table 3). Strauss and Corbin later conceded that "in the original development of grounded theory inductive aspects were overplayed" (Strauss & Corbin 1994, cited in Heath & Cowley, http://www.sxf.uevora.pt/wp-content/uploads/2013/03/Heath_2004.pdf).

## 4. The Three Contested Areas: Direct Comparison

### 4.1 Pre-existing theoretical frameworks in coding

| Glaser (1978) | Strauss & Corbin (1990) |
|---|---|
| Pre-existing frameworks contaminate emergence; the researcher should hold "as few predetermined thoughts as possible" (Glaser & Strauss, 1967; Glaser, 1978). | Researchers may—and should—bring accumulated disciplinary knowledge to coding; an "open mind" does not mean "an empty mind" (Strauss & Corbin, 1998). |
| Literature review is delayed; the only legitimate use of prior theory is *emergent fit*—comparing an emerging category with a pre-existing one and keeping only what fits the data (Glaser, 1978; Wuest, 2000, in Rieger, 2019). | Technical literature and disciplinary knowledge can legitimately sensitize the researcher and guide analysis from the start. |
| Coding families (e.g., the Six C's, 18+ theoretical code families) are sociological scaffolding to be deployed **after** open coding, when categories have already emerged (Glaser, 1978, 2005). | The coding paradigm is applied **during** axial coding—i.e., mid-analysis—to impose structure on the data. |

Kelle's (2007) assessment is the most precise available: Glaser's coding families are in fact "a hotchpotch" of formal and substantive concepts with no account of how they combine, whereas Strauss and Corbin's coding paradigm supplies a *specific*, if potentially constraining, skeleton of action—a difference between "a list of more or less related sociological and formal terms" versus "one general model of action" (https://d-nb.info/1186821515/34). A parallel German-language analysis (https://d-nb.info/1186823542/34) draws the sharp conclusion that Glaser's own position is *internally inconsistent*: "his stress on conceptual emergence and on refraining from using prior knowledge is inconsistent with his strong emphasis on using general social theoretical knowledge, represented in his coding families."

### 4.2 Legitimacy of forcing data into categories

| Glaser (1978, 1992) | Strauss & Corbin (1990) |
|---|---|
| "Emergence vs. forcing" became the title of the 1992 polemic; forcing is the cardinal methodological sin. Theory must be "discovered" via constant comparison alone. | The coding paradigm is explicitly a scaffold to organize messy data; structured coding is necessary to overcome the "common tendency [of novices] simply to take a bit of the data (a phrase or sentence or paragraph) and translate that into a précis of it" (Strauss, 1987, p. 29). |

Glaser's letter to Strauss, sent upon *Basics*' publication and incorporated in *Emergence vs. Forcing* (1992), read in part: "I request that you pull the book (*Basics of Qualitative Research*). It distorts and misconceives grounded theory, while engaging in a gross neglect of 90% of its important ideas…You wrote a whole different method so why call it 'grounded theory'?"—signed "your pal Barney" (Glaser, 1992, p. 2, cited in https://nsuworks.nova.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1416&context=tqr). He accused Strauss and Corbin of producing "conceptual description" rather than theory.

Heath and Cowley's (2004) close reading of the 1990 text substantiates the concern: "the theory is constructed under the control of a specified framework that now dictates coding to produce a linear model of causes, intervening conditions and consequences…These aspects of the theory may well be relevant but the accompanying threat that unless the model is used the theory will lack clarity and precision, increasingly forces the researcher towards this positivistic linearity" (http://www.sxf.uevora.pt/wp-content/uploads/2013/03/Heath_2004.pdf). They also note the ironic mechanism of code proliferation: the intense questioning techniques Strauss and Corbin recommend "extend far beyond the data to generate hundreds of codes and it is possible that it is this proliferation of codes that necessitates considerable reduction and thus the extra level of axial coding."

Strauss and Corbin answered in *Qualitative Sociology* (1998): "Alternative Interpretations," defending their use of structured coding as necessary for handling complexity, not forcing (https://exa.ai/library/publiccation/145crx4vtx7). They maintained that their procedures "were designed not to be used rigidly but creatively and flexibly by researchers as they deem appropriate" (Strauss & Corbin, 1990, p. 13). Walker and Myrick (2006) summarized the dispute as fundamentally about "the timing and level of researcher intervention" in coding—"with Glaser claiming that CGGT alone allows theory to emerge because it has no external frame until theoretical coding is conducted" (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1049732305285972).

Kelle (2007) concluded that Glaser's critique "points out some existing weaknesses of Strauss's concepts but vastly exaggerates the risks of the Straussian approach" (https://d-nb.info/1186821515/34). After 1991, the dispute became irretrievable: "the exchange of letters ensued with myself pleading and Anselm saying 'no' to a pulling and correction of Basics of Qualitative Research" (Glaser, 1992, p. 3, quoted in https://eprints.soton.ac.uk/16340/1/What_are_grounded_theories_made_of_28paper_29.pdf).

### 4.3 Verification procedures

| Glaser (1978, 1992) | Strauss & Corbin (1990) |
|---|---|
| Verification belongs to deductive/quantitative paradigms; in GT, constant comparison internally "assumes verification" but the goal is theory generation (Glaser & Strauss, 1967, p. 28). | Hypothesis-testing and verification of emerging theoretical claims are legitimate throughout the analytic process. |
| "The researcher who easily and persistently finds verification of ideas [should be] alert to the danger of forcing data" (Glaser, 1992, quoted in Heath & Cowley). | By 1998, "deduction followed by verification" had become "deduction followed by validation and elaboration from further data comparisons" (Strauss & Corbin 1998, cited in Heath & Cowley, http://www.sxf.uevora.pt/wp-content/uploads/2013/03/Heath_2004.pdf). |

The 1967 text was itself explicitly anti-verificationist: comparative analysis "both subsumes and assumes verification and accurate description, but only to the extent that the latter are in the services of generation" (Glaser & Strauss, 1967, p. 28; emphasized in Rieger, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6559166/). Kelle (2007) further argues that his refusal "unduly reduces the competitiveness and productivity of Grounded Theory-based analysis, whilst mistakenly seeing verification as bound to hypothetico-deductive approaches" (https://openurl.ebsco.com/contentitem/gcd:25092044?id=ebsco%3Agcd%3A25092044).

## 5. Charmaz's Constructivist Reformulation (2006)

Kathy Charmaz—Strauss's doctoral student at UCSF and trained in the first cohort under both founders—published *Constructing Grounded Theory: A Practical Guide through Qualitative Analysis* (Sage, 2006; 2nd ed. 2014; reported 3rd ed. October 2024, though posthumous status is unclear given Charmaz's death in July 2020). The book has accumulated approximately **60,209 Google Scholar citations** (https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Constructing+Grounded+Theory%3A+A+Practical+Guide+through+Qualitative+Analysis&publication_year=2006&author=K.+Charmaz; 13.4k indexed per https://www.rankless.org/hit-papers/w3111075), making it by an order of magnitude the single most cited monograph in grounded-theory methodology—roughly 2.5× Glaser's *Theoretical Sensitivity* (~24,252) and ~3.7× *Emergence vs. Forcing* (~16,002). Charmaz had h-index 64 and ~61,554 total citations at her death (https://exa.ai/library/publiccation/sppkd8gqk5s).

### 5.1 Epistemological Shift: From Objectivist Discovery to Constructivist Co-Construction

Charmaz repositioned GT squarely in social constructionism, rejecting the assumption embedded in the title *The Discovery of Grounded Theory*: "data and theorizing about these data…are constructed, not discovered" (Charmaz, 2017, https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1609406917719350). She argued that "neither the data nor the theories are discovered. Rather, we are part of the world we study and the data we collect" (Charmaz, 2006, p. 187). The researcher is "the author of a reconstruction of experience and meaning" (Mills, Bonner & Francis, 2006, https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/160940690600500103). Theory is "an interpretive portrayal of the studied world, not an exact picture of it" (Charmaz, 2006, p. 10, quoted in https://nsuworks.nova.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1365&context=tqr).

Her explicit epistemological grounds swap: "I saw no reason to discard these tools and every reason to shift the epistemological grounds on which researchers used them" (Charmaz, quoted at https://researchmethodscommunity.sagepub.com/blog/kathy-charmaz-1939-2020-developer-of-constructivist-grounded-theory). Charmaz's CGT "builds on its pragmatist heritage, shifts its epistemological foundations, and resolves contradictions in earlier versions of the method" (Charmaz, 2017, https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/1609406917719350). She located her pragmatist lineage explicitly in *Strauss's* philosophy of action while appropriating *Glaser's* methodological minimalism—a hybrid that tried to make the founding tension productive rather than fatal.

### 5.2 Resolution of the Three Contested Areas

**On pre-existing frameworks:** Charmaz sided with Strauss and Corbin against Glaser's tabula-rasa ideal, noting that "an increasing number of grounded theorists disagree" with Glaser's claim that researchers can enter the field without preconceptions; reading prior theory, for Charmaz, informs but does not determine interpretation (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/1609406917719350). She reframes this through *positional reflexivity* rather than procedural scaffolding.

**On forcing vs. emergence:** Charmaz adopted Glaser's flexible instincts, abolishing the axial coding/paradigm machinery through her simplified two-stage coding architecture (*initial coding*, then *focused coding*)—"a simplified, constructivist version of grounded theory" (Charmaz 2000, quoted in Thomas, https://pure-oai.bham.ac.uk/ws/files/2921100/Thomas_BriEdResJ_2006.pdf). However, she reconceptualizes "emergence" ontologically: codes and categories emerge *through the researcher's interpretive engagement with the data*, not as objective entities waiting to be found.

**On verification:** Charmaz replaced verification with *credibility, originality, resonance, and usefulness* as evaluative criteria (Charmaz, 2006, 2014; Rieger, 2018, Table 3), aligning with constructivist and interpretivist standards rather than positivist ones. She preserved constant comparison but relocated it under reflexivity: the researcher interrogates "data, nascent analyses, research actions, and themselves each step along the way" (Charmaz, 2017).

### 5.3 What Charmaz Retained

CGT preserved the core methodological *strategies* of the original—simultaneous data collection and analysis, constant comparison, coding, memo-writing, theoretical sampling, and theoretical saturation. Charmaz argued these are "methodological strategies" that can serve different epistemological positions, much as a hammer can be used in the service of different architectural visions (Charmaz, 2006; 2017).

### 5.4 Remaining Tension

A live philosophical question persists—whether the concept of "emergence" is sustainable within a constructivist frame (Bunniss & Kelly, 2017, *Educational Action Research*, https://doi.org/10.1080/09650792.2017.1365704). Critiques from Duchscher and Morgan (2004), Evans (2013), and Glaser (2002) view the constructivist turn as an erosion of GT's analytical power, as documented in Rieger (2019).

## 6. The "Paradigm Wars" Context (1990s–2000s)

The Glaser–Strauss–Charmaz sequence was embedded in—and shaped by—the larger "paradigm wars" of the period. According to the standard periodization (Teddlie & Tashakkori, 2003; Lincoln & Guba, 1985, 1994, 2000, 2005; Lincoln, Lynham & Guba, 2011; Denzin & Lincoln, 2011, https://us.sagepub.com/sites/default/files/upm-binaries/51015_ch_1.pdf):

1. **Postpositivist–constructivist war against positivism (1970–1990):** Ended symbolically with Guba's (1990) *The Paradigm Dialog*.
2. **Conflict among postpositivist, constructivist, and critical-theory paradigms (1990–2005):** The "handbook wars"—Denzin & Lincoln's *Handbook of Qualitative Research* editions (1994, 2000, 2005, 2011, 2018) became the canonical battlefield. Charmaz (2000) and Bryant & Charmaz (2007a, 2007b, 2007c) explicitly grounded their GT reformulation within this contested terrain (https://evallab.unm.edu/restricted-materials/sage-qual-research-2011-ch1.pdf).
3. **Evidence-based vs. mixed-methods/interpretive/critical schools (2005–present):** The current phase, marked by politicized disputes over "scientifically based research" (No Child Left Behind, post-2010 evidence-based movements).

Guba and Lincoln's canonical 1994 chapter mapped four competing paradigms—positivism, postpositivism, critical theory, constructivism—and observed that qualitative inquiry arose from "growing dissatisfaction with the patent overemphasis on quantitative methods," with paradigm viewed as the "basic belief system or worldview that guides the investigator" (https://ethnographyworkshop.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/11/guba-lincoln-1994-competing-paradigms-in-qualitative-research-handbook-of-qualitative-research.pdf). By the 2005 *Handbook* revision, Guba and Lincoln could report that "the number of qualitative texts, research papers, workshops, and training materials has exploded" and that "the legitimacy of postmodern paradigms is well established and at least equal to the legitimacy of received and conventional paradigms" (https://miguelangelmartinez.net/IMG/pdf/2018_denzin_lincoln_handbook_qualitative_research-213-263.pdf).

The Glaser/Strauss split is a paradigm war in miniature: postpositivist/objectivist classic GT (Glaser) versus pragmatist/symbolic-interactionist Straussian GT (Strauss & Corbin), with constructivist GT (Charmaz) attempting a paradigm-dialogue resolution. Charmaz's constructivist GT, introduced in the *Handbook* in 2000 ("Grounded Theory: Objectivist and Constructivist Methods," https://qualquant.org/wp-content/uploads/text/Charmaz%202000.pdf) and consolidated in the 2006 book, was thus not merely a methodological proposal but a deployment of the era's winning epistemological vocabulary. By 2018 the debate had matured into a recognized tripartite landscape: "classic Glaserian grounded theory, Straussian grounded theory, and constructivist grounded theory" are treated as "the most extensively developed and used" configurations (Rieger, 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6559166/).

## 7. Contemporary Dominance in Qualitative Training (2020–2024)

Empirical bibliometric evidence from recent reviews converges on three findings, though exact Scopus/Web of Science counts are not directly accessible and figures should be read with database-disclosure caveats.

### Finding 1: Charmaz's constructivist GT dominates nursing, library/information science, and social/health research methodology training

A 2023 review of three high-impact Library and Information Science journals (*Journal of Documentation*, *JASIST*, *Library & Information Science Research*) found that "Charmazian (constructivist) grounded theory approach was the most popular version," with grounded theory used predominantly as "a research design or methodology" employing constant comparative analysis (https://distantreader.org/stacks/journals-ojs/aliseacp/aliseacp-1297.pdf). Multiple 2020–2024 studies in nursing and health research methodology journals cite Charmaz (2006/2014) as their primary methodological reference (e.g., https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/16094069231186257).

### Finding 2: Straussian GT remains the procedural default in education, management, and information systems, but is losing ground

An 18-year review of 210 studies across 15 top education journals (DeClerq et al., 2021, https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/16094069211052203) concluded: "While educational researchers appear to prefer Straussian approaches to the design and analysis of grounded theory studies, Charmaz's constructivist approach has increased in popularity over the last decade." A Brazilian nursing journals study (Peiter et al., 2019, *Texto & Contexto Enfermagem* 28, https://doi.org/10.1590/1980-265X-TCE-2018-0177) found Straussian GT predominated at 79.6% of studies in Qualis A1/A2 journals (2013–2016). In management research's top four outlets (AMJ, ASQ, OS, SMJ), Strauss & Corbin (1990) received 123 citations across the corpus, Glaser (1992) received 3, and Charmaz (2006) received 22—indicating the Strauss & Corbin volume remains the primary procedural reference in management (Walsh et al., adapted, https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/abas/18/2/18_0190326a/_pdf, Table 1). An IS-field study found that "Straussian grounded theory procedures—which have found most adherents in the IS discipline—are utilized" extensively (https://aisel.aisnet.org/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1960&context=jit). Makri & Neely (2021), "Grounded Theory: A Guide for Exploratory Studies in Management Research," https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/16094069211013654, similarly documents the Straussian procedural dominance.

### Finding 3: Pure Glaserian GT has negligible presence in mainstream methodology journals

Across disciplines, OpenAlex and Google Scholar both show that *Theoretical Sensitivity* and *Emergence vs. Forcing* are cited overwhelmingly in methodological discussion and historiography of GT, not as primary references for new empirical work. Glaserian GT persists as a vigorous but self-consciously orthodox minority, sustained by the Grounded Theory Institute, its journal *Grounded Theory Review*, and Sociology Press (Rieger, 2019; https://groundedtheoryreview.org/index.php/gtr/article/view/413). The *Grounded Theory Review*'s own recent literature—including the 2018 essay weighing "Classic GT or Constructivist GT"—concedes that "valid arguments could be made to support Classic and Constructive GT approaches," a defensive posture characteristic of a tradition that no longer sets the agenda (https://groundedtheoryreview.org/index.php/gtr/article/view/291).

### Quantitative Summary Table (citation counts, late 2024)

| Work | Google Scholar (approx.) | OpenAlex |
|---|---|---|
| Charmaz (2006/2014), *Constructing Grounded Theory* | ~60,209 | — |
| Strauss & Corbin (1990), *Basics of Qualitative Research* (all eds.) | tens of thousands | — |
| Glaser (1978), *Theoretical Sensitivity* | ~24,252 | ~6,120 |
| Glaser (1992), *Emergence vs. Forcing* | ~16,002 | ~2,884 |

(Note: the Google Scholar vs. OpenAlex discrepancy for *Theoretical Sensitivity*—~24,252 vs. ~6,120, a roughly 4× gap—reflects different database snapshots and inclusion rules, not data conflict. Author-level h-indices/citation totals also differ across databases: one source reports Glaser h-index 49/~149,000 citations vs. Strauss h-index 55/~205,000—a ~1.38× Strauss advantage (https://exa.ai/library/publiccation/sppkd8gqk5s)—while another reports Corbin h-index 36/~148,368 and Charmaz h-index 64/~61,554. These figures use different baselines and cannot be cleanly reconciled.)

### Synthesis

Charmaz's constructivist GT now dominates qualitative methodology training programs in nursing, education, library science, sociology, social work, and health-research methodology courses, as evidenced by (a) citation asymmetry in 2020–2024 methodology journals; (b) the explicit findings of the DeClerq et al. (2021) 18-year education journal review and the 2023 LIS review; and (c) the institutional embedding of *Constructing Grounded Theory* in third-edition course adoptions (Sage, October 2024, https://uk.sagepub.com/en-gb/hkg/constructing-grounded-theory/book255601). Crucially, the *Basics of Qualitative Research* franchise itself has drifted toward constructionism: Corbin & Strauss (2008, 2015) "move[d] away from post-positivism... toward explicit constructionism" (Charmaz 2014, https://us2.sagepub.com/sites/default/files/upm-binaries/61018_Charmaz__Reconstructing_Grounded_Theory.pdf), meaning that the most widely assigned Straussian text now teaches a position much closer to Charmaz's than to the 1990 original. Straussian GT persists as the procedural default in management, IS, and a portion of educational and nursing research, while Glaser's classic GT is confined to a specialized methodological-historical niche.

## 8. Conclusion

The Glaser–Strauss debate of the late 1980s and 1990s was not merely procedural but paradigmatic: it staged the encounter between residual positivism, pragmatist symbolic interactionism, and the emerging constructivist turn. Charmaz's 2006 reformulation effectively absorbed the legitimate concerns of all sides—the Strauss/Corbin acknowledgement that researchers cannot enter the field empty-headed, the Glaserian insistence that data should not be forced into pre-existing categories, and the post-1990s consensus that researchers are not external observers of an objective reality—while relocating the entire enterprise within social constructionism. The result, judged by 2020–2024 citation patterns in major methodology journals, is the contemporary dominance of constructivist grounded theory in qualitative research training programs—particularly in nursing, social work, library/information science, and health-research methodology—with Straussian GT holding a substantial but declining procedural foothold in management, IS, and parts of applied education and nursing, and pure Glaserian GT confined to a specialized methodological-historical niche sustained by the Grounded Theory Institute and *Grounded Theory Review*. The methodological split has never been fully resolved—and perhaps should not be—because the three positions correspond to genuinely different answers to foundational epistemological questions: Can theory be "discovered" in data? Is verification inherent in the analytic process? Can researcher subjectivity be disciplined or must it be reflexively embraced? What is clear is that the grounded theory debates have been among the most productive methodological controversies in the social sciences, forcing a discipline-wide reckoning with epistemology, researcher positionality, and the relationship between data and theory that extends well beyond the method itself.

# Comprehensive Literature Review: WISC-V versus NEPSY-II for ADHD Diagnosis in Children Ages 8–12 — Working Memory Sensitivity and Ecological Validity

## 1. Scope and Operational Definitions

This review addresses two focal questions for the 8–12 age band: (a) which instrument better detects working-memory (WM) deficits in ADHD, and (b) how pediatric neuropsychologists evaluate the ecological validity (EV) of the NEPSY-II relative to the WISC-V. A critical disambiguation must precede the synthesis: **"sensitivity" has at least three distinct psychometric senses**, and divergent comparative claims in the literature typically reflect answers to different questions rather than substantive disagreement.

| Sense of "sensitivity" | Definition | Typical finding for these instruments |
|---|---|---|
| **(a) Statistical** — group discrimination | Between-group effect size (*d*, Hedges' *g*) for ADHD vs. controls | WISC-V WMI: *d* ≈ 0.50–1.06; NEPSY-II EF subtests: *d* ≈ 0.30–0.80 (limited data) |
| **(b) Diagnostic** — case-finding | Proportion of true ADHD cases scoring "abnormal"; AUC | WISC-V WMI: AUC ≈ 0.46–0.64; NEPSY-II: not formally established |
| **(c) Incremental** — added value | Whether the measure predicts ADHD beyond rating scales/interview | ~zero for both cognitive batteries alone (Toplak et al., 2013, *JCPP* 54(2):131–143, http://www.keithstanovich.com/Site/Research_on_Reasoning_files/ToplakWestStanovich_2013.pdf) |

The Clinical Neuropsychologist 2020 review explicitly notes that cognitive test batteries show "inadequate sensitivity and specificity in identifying ADHD" (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13854046.2019.1696409); the 2023 *Assessment* review of 29 studies concluded that "measures of intellectual and executive functioning did not show incremental validity in the diagnosis of ADHD" (https://sage.cnpereading.com/doi/10.1177/10731911231159933).

## 2. Search Strategy

Systematic queries were executed on Google Scholar, PubMed/PMC, PsycINFO-indexed outlets, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, MDPI, and journal-specific repositories. Search strings combined instrument names ("WISC-V," "NEPSY-II," "WISC-IV") with diagnostic terms ("ADHD," "diagnosis," "diagnostic validity"), construct terms ("working memory," "executive function," "Cognitive Proficiency Index"), and methodological terms ("ecological validity," "meta-analysis," "sensitivity," "specificity," "measurement invariance"). Seminal theoretical papers (Barkley, 1997; Rapport et al., 2001; Korkman, Kirk, & Kemp, 2007), influential meta-analyses (Martinussen et al., 2005; Willcutt et al., 2005; Kasper, Alderson, & Hudec, 2012; Kofler et al., 2020; Pievsky & McGrath, 2018; Fried et al., 2024), recent empirical comparisons (Newberry, 2024/2025; BMC Psychology 2026; MDPI 2021/2025), and key methodological/critical reviews (Toplak, West, & Stanovich, 2013; Krasny-Pacini & Chevignard, 2024) were prioritized. The single direct head-to-head pediatric ADHD study (Newberry, 2025) is weighted accordingly and clearly flagged as unpublished.

## 3. Theoretical Frameworks

Four frameworks structure the literature:

1. **Barkley's Behavioral Inhibition Model (1997, *Psychological Bulletin* 121:65–94)** — Barkley posits that deficient response inhibition produces secondary impairments in four executive functions, of which WM is paramount. The paper has been cited >6,000 times and remains the most invoked framework in ADHD neuropsychology (https://dconducta.es/assets/barkley1997.pdf).

2. **Rapport, Chung, Shore, & Isaacs's Working-Memory Model (2001, *Journal of Learning Disabilities*)** — This competing model reorients causal priority: WM deficits are hypothesized central, with disinhibition as a downstream consequence (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/082957350401700503).

3. **Baddeley's Multi-Component Model** — Operationalizes WM as a central executive with phonological and visuospatial subsystems (Martinussen, Hayden, Hogg-Johnson, & Tannock, 2005, *JAACAP* 44(4):377–384, https://www.jaacap.org/article/S0890-8567(09)61489-1/abstract). The model is foundational because the WISC-V WMI samples verbal modalities heavily, while the largest ADHD–control effects emerge in spatial storage and central-executive domains.

4. **Luria's Functional-Systems Theory** — Underwrites the NEPSY-II's subtest-level architecture: "assessing a cognitive disorder requires separately assessing all the components that make up a functional system" (*Journal of Pediatric Neuropsychology*, 2024, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40817-024-00158-8). The NEPSY-II authors explicitly argue that factor analysis is incompatible with Lurian theory, **pre-emptively rejecting the psychometric standard by which the WISC-V is judged** and rendering head-to-head comparison philosophically asymmetric.

A contested meta-theory must be acknowledged: Barkley documents that the EF construct "lacks a consensus theory," with "more than 20 definitions" and "up to 33 components" attributed by experts (https://www.vapsych.org/assets/docs/Theory%20of%20Executive%20Function%20%20Self%20Regulation%20-%20Barkley.pdf). Any manuscript must therefore state which model is adopted because the two instruments operationalize WM differently: WISC-V treats WM as a factor-analytically derived composite; NEPSY-II treats it as content-valid subtest performance interpreted through Lurian theory.

## 4. WISC-V: Architecture, Working Memory Assessment, and ADHD Sensitivity

### 4.1 Structure
The WISC-V provides five primary indices: Verbal Comprehension (VCI), Visual-Spatial (VSI), Fluid Reasoning (FRI), Working Memory (WMI), and Processing Speed (PSI), plus ancillary composites including Cognitive Proficiency Index (CPI = WMI + PSI), General Ability Index (GAI), Auditory Working Memory Index (AWMI), and Nonverbal Index (NVI) (Pearson WISC-V Canadian FAQs, https://www.pearsonclinical.ca/content/dam/school/global/clinical/ca/assets/wisc-v-cdn/wisc-v-cdn-faqs.pdf; MDPI *Sustainability* 13(17):9948, https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/13/17/9948). The WMI comprises Digit Span (forward + backward + sequencing), Letter-Number Sequencing, with Picture Span as a supplementary visual subtest.

### 4.2 Group Discrimination — Large, Consistent Effects
- **Martin et al. (2023, *L'Année Psychologique* 123(4):613–638; n = 30 ADHD vs. 29 controls, ages 8–12):** WMI *d* = 1.178 (*p* < .001), PSI *d* = 1.125, Cognitive Skills Index *d* = 1.140 — all highly significant.
- **Tallberg et al. (Kindheit und Entwicklung 27(3), 2018; n = 103 ADHD, German):** Largest effect sizes on WM, fluid reasoning, and FSIQ; WISC-V characterized as a "valid and sensitive instrument" for ADHD cognitive profiles (https://econtent.hogrefe.com/doi/pdf/10.1026/0942-5403/a000256).
- **García-Mieres et al. (Actas Españolas de Psiquiatría 54(3), 2026; n = 188, ages 6–16):** Significantly lower WMI (*p* < .001), PSI (*p* < .001), CPI (*p* < .001), FSIQ (*p* = .005); logistic regression: WMI (B = −0.067, *p* < .001), PSI (B = −0.043, *p* = .007), CPI (B = −0.091, *p* < .001) predicted ADHD group membership. ADHD-I subgroup showed lower WMI than ADHD-C (*p* = .016) (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42343738/).
- **MDPI *Behavioral Sciences* 15(9):1279 (WISC-IV, n = 719):** VCI, PRI, WMI, PSI classified group membership with Nagelkerke R² = 0.44; lower WMI and PSI increased ADHD likelihood (https://www.mdpi.com/2076-328X/15/9/1279).
- **Martínez-García et al. (BMC Psychology 2026, n = 241, ages 6–17):** Confirmed a four-factor higher-order solution as best-fitting; WMI and PSI were significantly lower in ADHD with medium-to-large effect sizes relative to VCI, VSI, and FRI; CPI was significantly lower than GAI (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40359-026-05191-0).

### 4.3 Meta-Analytic Quantitative Synthesis
- **Martinussen et al. (2005) — the field-defining WM/ADHD meta-analysis.** 26 studies. Spatial storage *d* = 0.85 (95% CI 0.62–1.08); spatial central executive *d* = 1.06 (0.72–1.39); verbal storage *d* = 0.47 (0.36–0.59); verbal central executive *d* = 0.43 (0.24–0.62). Deficits were independent of comorbidity with language learning disorders and general intellectual ability (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15782085/).
- **Willcutt, Doyle, Nigg, Faraone, & Pennington (2005, *Biological Psychiatry* 57(11):1336–1346; 83 studies; ADHD n = 3,734, non-ADHD n = 2,969):** Effect sizes in medium range (.46–.69); strongest and most consistent effects on response inhibition, vigilance, WM, and planning; "EF weaknesses are neither necessary nor sufficient to cause all cases of ADHD" (https://www.biologicalpsychiatryjournal.com/article/S0006-3223(05)00171-X/abstract).
- **Kasper, Alderson, & Hudec (2012, *Clinical Psychology Review* 32(7):605–617):** "Large between-group effect sizes across both working memory domains"; significant moderators: percent female, number of experimental trials, recall vs. recognition format, central-executive demands (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0272735812000979).
- **Fried et al. (2024, *European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry*):** Largest meta-analysis of verbal WM (Digit Span Backward) in ADHD — 49 studies, n = 4,956 ADHD vs. n = 3,249 controls. Hedges' *g* = 0.56 (95% CI [0.49, 0.64]); effect size **decreased by 0.05 per additional year of age**, indicating WM deficits attenuate with development (https://www.ingentaconnect.com/content/routledg/clin/2020/00000034/00000005/art00002).
- **Pievsky & McGrath (2018):** Umbrella review of 37 meta-analyses; WM is the **second-largest ADHD-related neurocognitive deficit after reaction-time variability**, weighted mean SMD ≈ 0.54 (https://exa.ai/library/publication/bkyymp4jqzv).
- **Kofler et al. (2020, *Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society*; bifactor-(s-1) decomposition in 172 children ages 8–13):** When measurement unreliability is properly modeled, **central executive WM impairments reach *d* = 1.63–2.03, with 75–81% of ADHD children impaired**; smaller visuospatial STM impairment (*d* = 0.60, 38%); no phonological STM deficit (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5743590/). This reframes the WMI's poor classification accuracy as partly a measurement artifact rather than a true deficit in construct relevance.

### 4.4 Diagnostic Accuracy — Substantially Modest
- **Devena & Watkins (2012):** GAI–CPI discrepancy AUC = 0.64 (hospital ADHD vs. normative), 0.46 (hospital ADHD vs. referred non-diagnosed), 0.63 (school ADHD vs. normative), 0.50 (school ADHD vs. matched) — "low accuracy in identifying children with ADHD."
- **A 2025 cross-validated study (PubMed 42501447; n = 133, ages 6–16):** Multinomial logistic regression with leave-one-out cross-validation achieved only **32% accuracy** across ADHD, SLD, ADHD+SLD, and control groups — barely above chance. Authors advocate a "shared-vulnerability framework" and warn against disorder-specific interpretation of GAI–CPI discrepancies (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42501447/).
- **Iran J Psychiatry Behav Sci 2025 (n = 250 ADHD + 250 controls, ages 7–9; Iranian sample using "Davis scatter-diagram"):** Only Processing Speed subtests (Coding, Symbol Search, Random Cancellation, Structural Cancellation) exceeded critical thresholds (*p* < .001); **WM, verbal comprehension, visual-spatial, and fluid reasoning subtests failed to distinguish ADHD from controls** (https://brieflands.com/journals/ijpbs/articles/153741.pdf). The study is limited by single-site Iranian sampling and non-random selection.
- **Maherpub/JNDD 2025 (WISC-V Extended, n = 240; Iranian):** WM subtests (Spatial Span Forward/Backward, Sentence Recall) and Processing Speed subtests (Coding Recall, Coding Copy, Symbol Deletion) exceeded critical values; Symbol Deletion was the most sensitive single subtest (https://maherpub.com/index.php/jndd/article/view/514).
- **Population-level data (PubMed 36780371, WISC-IV WMI in 7–8-year-olds, n = 865):** 22% of children had WM deficits, but the majority of these did **not** have elevated behavioral regulation or hyperactivity/inattention problems; only 4% had both. About one-third of those with combined WM and BR/HI problems met inattentive ADHD criteria — underscoring that low WMI is neither necessary nor sufficient for an ADHD diagnosis (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36780371/).

### 4.5 Measurement Invariance Constraint
**Schwarze et al. (2024; PMC10817318) — MGCFA on German WISC-V, n = 91 ADHD vs. 91 controls:** Configural and metric invariance were supported, but only **partial scalar invariance** was achieved; the ADHD group scored lower on four primary subtests (Digit Span, Coding, Symbol Search, Picture Span — the very subtests composing the WM and PS indices), producing lower WMI, PSI, and FSIQ. The authors caution that interpretation of WISC-V primary indexes in ADHD samples is constrained by this partial invariance (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38248904/ and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10817318/). **This finding is particularly consequential: it suggests that observed WMI differences between ADHD and non-ADHD groups may partly reflect measurement artifacts rather than true latent differences.**

### 4.6 Methodological Vulnerability — Digit Span Administration
**Kofler, Wells, et al. (2017; *JINS*; n = 45 ADHD vs. 41 controls, ages 8–13):** Standard WISC-style Digit Span administration has weak construct validity for working memory because of the discontinue rule. **Alternate scoring — counting all digits correct rather than trials correct — raised correlations with WM reordering from non-significant to *r* = .58**, and correlations with academic achievement reached *r* = .49 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5743590/). This finding applies to WISC-V WMI administration as well and is a direct, actionable methodological intervention: minor scoring changes markedly improve sensitivity.

### 4.7 Subcomponent Pattern — "Good Holders, Bad Shufflers"
A 2024 *JINS* analysis demonstrated that children with ADHD, especially ADHD-Inattentive, are differentially poorer on backward (manipulation) than forward (maintenance) and on visual-spatial than auditory-verbal spans (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-international-neuropsychological-society/article/abs/good-holders-bad-shufflers-an-examination-of-working-memory-processes-and-modalities). The Frontiers in Psychiatry 2024 occupy-WM study showed that occupying WM capacity slowed RTs and reduced accuracy on inhibition tasks in ADHD vs. anxious children (*d* = 0.50–1.53), providing "strong evidence against" the claim that WM deficits are secondary to inhibition deficits (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychiatry/articles/10.3389/fpsyt.2024.1277583/full). Kofler et al. (2019, *Neuropsychology*) used within-subject experimental design with 41 children to demonstrate directional effects: increasing WM demands significantly reduced information processing speed (BF₁₀ = 5.82 × 10⁹⁶), whereas experimentally reducing processing speed did not significantly affect WM performance (BF₀₁ = 1.31) — strong evidence that WM deficits are upstream of processing speed deficits in ADHD.

## 5. NEPSY-II: Architecture and ADHD Sensitivity

### 5.1 Structure
The NEPSY-II (Korkman, Kirk, & Kemp, 2007) revised and expanded the 1998 NEPSY from 27 subtests (ages 3–12) to **32 subtests (ages 3–16)**, organized into six theoretically derived domains: Attention/Executive Functioning, Language, Sensorimotor, Visuospatial Processing, Memory and Learning, and Social Perception (https://catalogimages.wiley.com/images/db/pdf/9780470436912.excerpt.pdf). The Attention/EF domain contains Animal Sorting (concept formation, set-shifting), Auditory Attention (sustained auditory vigilance), Response Set (alternating set-shifting under inhibitory demands), Inhibition (Naming/Inhibition/Switching), Clocks (planning/organization), Design Fluency, Word Generation, and Statue (https://www.wiley.com/en-us/Essentials+of+NEPSY-II+Assessment-p-9780470634639).

### 5.2 Critical Architectural Asymmetry
Three facts from the Pearson NEPSY-II manual decisively constrain the comparison (https://www.pearsonassessments.com/content/dam/school/global/clinical/us/assets/nepsy-ii/nepsy-ii-design-and-purpose.pdf):
- "The domains are theoretically, not statistically, derived."
- "Domain scores are not derived in the NEPSY-II due to these psychometric issues and the clinical sensitivity and utility of the individual subtest scores."
- "Subtests within a domain may not correlate highly with one another."

**The net effect: NEPSY-II cannot produce a working-memory index.** The WISC-V can. Any "NEPSY-II working memory sensitivity" claim in the literature is therefore a claim about isolated subtests (Word List Interference, Sentence Repetition, Memory for Designs), not about a validated index.

A specific, arguable capacity reduction in the NEPSY-II for ADHD-relevant EF assessment: **the revision removed the Tower planning subtest** — precisely the domain Willcutt et al. (2005) found among the strongest ADHD effects (planning *d* in the .46–.69 band; https://www.biologicalpsychiatryjournal.com/article/S0006-3223(05)00171-X/abstract). Planning/organizing a complex response was added as a subcomponent within other subtests, but the dedicated planning measure was eliminated (Broz, Avirett, Maricle, & Miller, Texas Woman's University, https://twu-ir.tdl.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/cd5d9abc-ac46-4a2a-b0e9-e0689da46eb1/content).

### 5.3 Validity Evidence in ADHD and Related Samples
- **Gallo et al. (2025, *Children* 12(6):798; n = 48 children 8–15; ADHD vs. anxiety disorder vs. ADHD + anxiety; WISC-IV + NEPSY-II + MASC-2):** No significant group differences emerged in cognitive performance, attention, or **working memory**; significant differences emerged only on **inhibition**, with anxiety-disorder children more efficient than ADHD or ADHD+AD groups (https://www.mdpi.com/2227-9067/12/6/798). **This is the only directly relevant study on working memory sensitivity of the NEPSY-II in a clinical sample**, and it found no group WM differences — a finding that complicates claims of NEPSY-II superiority for WM sensitivity specifically.
- **Davis & Matthews (2010, *Journal of Psychoeducational Assessment*, cited 74 times):** Reviewed reliability and validity evidence; characterized NEPSY-II as comprehensive but cautious about subtest-level interpretation; flagged concerns over the standardization sample representation (https://exa.ai/library/publication/1fs8mqkt0rv).
- **Matthews & Davis (2010, *Child Neuropsychology*):** Comprehensive assessment across functions and modalities; strong age-appropriate norms but variable subtest reliability (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/09297040903146966).
- **Brooks et al. (2024, *Child Neuropsychology*):** Confirmatory factor analysis of the NEPSY-II norming sample (n = 600, ages 7–12) found that the best-fitting model included a general factor and four first-order factors — departing from the six-domain structure. General factor loadings for most subtests were < .50 (range .21–.69, M = .44); subtest-specific effects were even lower. **All subtests demonstrated strong subtest-specific effects, "but it is not clear what construct(s) the subtest-specific effects represent."**
- **J Pediatr Neuropsychol 2024 EFA of the NEPSY-II Conceptual Template:** Six-factor model best represented the data for the 7–12-year-old group, broadly supporting the conceptual domains; but Social Perception subtests in particular require cautious interpretation because that latent dimension could not be reliably located (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40817-024-00158-8).
- **Cardinal Scholar (2015; n = clinical, WISC-IV + NEPSY-II):** Canonical correlations were generally non-significant between WISC-IV composites and NEPSY-II Inhibition, suggesting clinically-referred children show weaker WMI/PSI–EF coupling than healthy children; however, the WM and PS tasks of the WISC-IV were significantly related to NEPSY-II Inhibition-Naming and Inhibition-Switching Combined scores (https://cardinalscholar.bsu.edu/items/1393f480-5723-49c0-b220-23237bd85e25).

## 6. Direct Head-to-Head Comparison: Newberry (2024/2025)

The single most pertinent direct comparison is **Newberry, K. E. (2025). *Pay Attention! A Comparative Analysis of Psychological Assessments and Neurological Mechanisms for ADHD Within a Pediatric Population* (PsyD dissertation, Antioch University Seattle; April 2025)** (https://aura.antioch.edu/etds/1127/; https://etd.ohiolink.edu/acprod/odb_etd/ws/send_file/send?accession=antioch1744236100254081&disposition=inline).

- **Sample:** 272 children aged **8–16** in archival data; grouped by ADHD subtype (Inattentive, Combined/Hyperactive, or no diagnosis).
- **Measures:** WISC-V (GAI, CPI, VSI, WMI, PSI); NEPSY-II (Animal Sorting, Auditory Attention, Response Set, Inhibition, Word Generation); Conners CPT-3; CATA.
- **Analyses:** Binary and multinomial logistic regressions controlling for gender.
- **Key findings:** (a) Lower CPI and lower NEPSY-II Animal Sorting and Response Set significantly predicted any ADHD diagnosis vs. no diagnosis; (b) Higher CATA scores predicted lower likelihood of Inattentive and Combined/Hyperactive ADHD; (c) the WISC-V WMI in isolation was not a robust predictor; (d) the NEPSY-II contributed incremental validity beyond the WISC-V.
- **Author's conclusion (verbatim):** "These results support using NEPSY-II, CATA, and CPT-3 for targeted, efficient ADHD assessments over traditional tools like the WISC-V. Streamlining batteries could improve diagnostic accuracy, reduce testing time, and enhance accessibility."

**Critical caveats — non-negotiable for peer review:**
1. The dissertation is a PsyD project, not a peer-reviewed journal article, and has not been indexed in major bibliographic databases. **Treat as hypothesis-generating, not confirmatory.**
2. The sample age range is 8–16, which overlaps but **extends beyond the requested 8–12 range**; age-stratified analyses are not provided.
3. Archival, cross-sectional data limit causal inference.
4. The single-study nature means no independent replication exists; the finding has not been subjected to peer review.
5. The logistic regression framework does not yield traditional sensitivity/specificity or AUC metrics that would permit direct comparison with the broader diagnostic-accuracy literature.

## 7. Working-Memory Sensitivity — Synthesis

**Sense (a) — statistical group discrimination:** The WISC-V WMI wins decisively. The WISC-V WMI effect sizes for ADHD vs. typically developing comparisons cluster at *d* = 0.50–1.06 (Martinussen et al., 2005 meta-analytic estimates for spatial/central executive components, with substantial extension to higher *d* = 1.6–2.0 when measurement unreliability is properly modeled — Kofler et al., 2020). The WISC-V WMI directly measures both storage and manipulation of verbal and visual content. The NEPSY-II lacks a WM composite and the only relevant clinical data (Gallo et al., 2025) found no significant WM group differences on the NEPSY-II between ADHD, anxiety, and comorbid groups.

**Sense (b) — diagnostic classification:** Neither instrument is adequate. Cognitive batteries show "inadequate sensitivity and specificity" (Sjowall et al., *Clin Neuropsychol* 2020, https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13854046.2019.1696409); cross-validated classification accuracy for WISC-V in ADHD is barely above chance (32%, PubMed 42501447); AUC values for GAI–CPI discrepancy are 0.46–0.64 (Devena & Watkins, 2012); population data show low WMI is neither necessary nor sufficient for ADHD (PubMed 36780371). NEPSY-II ADHD diagnostic-accuracy data are sparser still.

**Sense (c) — incremental validity:** The single available head-to-head study (Newberry, 2025) found that NEPSY-II Animal Sorting and Response Set, **but not the WISC-V WMI**, were significant independent predictors of ADHD diagnosis in regression models controlling for gender. This is the best available evidence for NEPSY-II's incremental-validity advantage, **but it rests on a single unpublished study extending to age 16 and must be treated as hypothesis-generating.**

**Mechanistic accounts of the NEPSY-II's potential incremental-validity advantage** (from Panel 1 analysis):
1. Modality coverage — the NEPSY-II's Attention/EF subtests include visual, auditory, and switching demands, whereas WISC-V WMI is heavily weighted toward auditory-verbal channels with only Picture Span representing visual.
2. Subcomponent granularity — the NEPSY-II distinguishes maintenance (Auditory Attention), manipulation (Inhibition-Switching), set-shifting (Response Set), and concept formation (Animal Sorting) — closer to Baddeley's central executive, where ADHD–control effects are largest.
3. Test impurity and ecological content — NEPSY-II subtests include game-like, multi-step procedures more sensitive to real-world executive breakdown.

**However,** the Kofler/Wells Digit Span administration finding (standard discontinue rules systematically under-detect WM deficits; *r* jumps from non-significant to .58 with modified scoring) applies to WISC-V and **largely dissolves the apparent NEPSY-II advantage**: if WISC-V WMI is rescored per Wells et al. (2017), both instruments may yield comparable incremental validity, but no published study has tested this empirically.

**Verdict on WM sensitivity for ages 8–12:**
- For **narrow WM construct** (storage + manipulation of verbal/visual information): **WISC-V WMI** — better psychometric precision, larger documented effect sizes, normed index available.
- For **broader EF profile** of ADHD (inhibition, set-shifting, switching, plus WM components): **NEPSY-II Attention/EF subtests** (Animal Sorting, Response Set, Inhibition-Switching) — more comprehensive coverage and superior incremental validity in the single available head-to-head study.
- For **classifying individual children**: **neither instrument alone**.

## 8. Ecological Validity

### 8.1 Conceptual Foundations
A 2024 systematic review in the *Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society* (Krasny-Pacini & Chevignard, https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-international-neuropsychological-society/article/conceptualization-of-the-term-ecological-validity-in-neuropsychological-research-on-executive-function-assessment/01C595F6F8931798F9053A0628260BA0) found that of 90+ EF studies claiming EV, only 31% provided a formal definition. The field conflates veridical/criterion validity (prediction of real-world behavior), verisimilitude/face validity (similarity to real-world tasks), and sensitivity/specificity. The authors call for replacement of "ecological validity" with concrete terms such as "criterion validity." A 2023 systematized review by Pinto, Dores, Peixoto, & Barbosa operationalizes EV along two dimensions — **representativeness** (artificial↔natural, simple↔complex) and **generalization** (statistical prediction to everyday functioning) — and proposes a six-stage EV-checklist (https://exa.ai/library/publication/2xb6brjjgpy). A 2012 review in *Applied Neuropsychology: Child* noted that EV research in pediatric neuropsychology is far less developed than in adult neuropsychology (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/21622965.2012.686330).

The scholarly standard for ecological-validity claims in this review is therefore the **Pinto et al. (2023) representativeness × generalization framework**, not the loose usage critiqued in Krasny-Pacini & Chevignard (2024).

### 8.2 EV Placement of Each Instrument
By the Pinto framework:
- **WISC-V WMI** subtests (Digit Span, Letter-Number Sequencing, Picture Span) are **high on artificiality, low on naturalism**: standardized, time-limited, single-modality, minimal distraction, social demand, or task-switching. Their EV for predicting classroom behavior, homework completion, or peer functioning rests almost entirely on **criterion (predictive) validity studies** (Kofler et al.; Rapport et al.).
- **NEPSY-II** Inhibition (Naming/Switching), Animal Sorting, Response Set, and Auditory Attention subtests are **more naturalistic in verisimilitude**: they include game-like materials, multi-step instructions, set-switching, and distractor conditions that more closely resemble real-world classroom demands. The Inhibition subtest in particular requires children to suppress automatic responses under time pressure — a scenario with face validity for classroom behavior regulation.

**However — a critical caveat:** both instruments are administered in the same structured, 1:1 clinical environment and thus **share the same fundamental structured-environment limitation**. The Simpson et al. (2024, *The Clinical Neuropsychologist*, doi: 10.1080/20590776.2024.2412336) rapid review noted that "cognitive assessments are completed in quiet, structured, 1:1 environments that, while essential to the manualised administration of the test, do not reflect daily environments that children are subject to including conflicting attentional demands." The authors concluded "there is little clinical utility to undertake a WISC-V in all ADHD assessment cases." Torres van Grinsven (2022) argued that this testing environment may not produce scores "truly indicative of the child's ability" in naturalistic settings.

### 8.3 Reviews by Pediatric Neuropsychologists on EV
**No published head-to-head EV study directly comparing WISC-V and NEPSY-II in pediatric ADHD was located.** The available reviews characterize each instrument separately:
- **Matthews & Davis (2010); Davis & Matthews (2010); reviews summarized in *Essentials of NEPSY-II Assessment*, Brooks, Sherman, & Strauss:** Characterize the NEPSY-II as offering better cross-domain and cross-modality assessment within one normed battery, which in principle supports stronger treatment planning and prediction of daily functioning (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0734282909346716). Same reviews caution that the NEPSY-II's structure has not been independently factor-analyzed until recently and that subtest-level interpretation should be cautious in the Social Perception domain.
- **For the WISC-V:** The Toplak, West, & Stanovich (2013, *JCPP* 54(2):131–143) review of 20 studies comparing performance-based and rating measures of executive function found that **only 24% of 286 correlations were statistically significant**, with an **overall median correlation of only *r* = .19** — meaning performance-based measures and rating scales assess different underlying mental constructs. Toplak et al. (2008) demonstrated that when both were examined as predictors of ADHD status, parent and teacher ratings entered as significant predictors while **performance-based measures accounted for little unique variance in predicting ADHD status**. The correlation is sometimes cited as ≈.30 with ≈9% shared variance; the more precise figure from the review is the median *r* = .19, representing less than 4% shared variance.
- **Barkley (2012, *Executive Functions*, Guilford):** Argues that ADHD should be reconceptualized as a disorder of EF assessed through "real-world" measures rather than performance-based tests alone; characterizes EF tests as having "very low or no ecological validity" (https://www.guilford.com/excerpts/barkley20.pdf).

**Verdict on ecological validity:** The NEPSY-II is, by expert consensus and by the Pinto verisimilitude framework, the **more ecologically valid instrument in design** — but EV in the strict predictive sense has been under-studied for both instruments in pediatric ADHD. **The NEPSY-II's EV advantage rests on task-design arguments (verisimilitude), not on predictive-validity data.** The WISC-V's strengths (standardization, large normative sample, broad cognitive coverage) make it a **better norm-referenced tool but not necessarily a better predictor of real-world functioning**.

**Common methodological concerns across the literature:**
1. **Cross-sectional design in all studies**: no longitudinal data tracking how scores predict later ADHD diagnosis.
2. **Criterion contamination**: most studies use DSM-based clinical diagnoses as gold standard, which are behaviorally rather than neuropsychologically defined.
3. **Age band heterogeneity**: most cited studies use broader age bands (6–16, 6–17, 7–12); the Newberry dissertation specifically extends to age 16, yet none of the reviewed studies provide age-stratified analyses within the specific 8–12 range requested.
4. **Limited NEPSY-II ADHD specificity data**: few studies have examined NEPSY-II sensitivity/specificity for ADHD specifically.
5. **Comorbidity confounds**: many studies fail to adequately control for comorbid learning disabilities, anxiety, and other conditions.
6. **Single critical comparison**: the Newberry dissertation is the only direct WISC-V/NEPSY-II comparison and has not been independently replicated.
7. **No head-to-head EV study exists**: ecological validity studies comparing WISC-V and NEPSY-II predictions to real-world functional outcomes in ADHD are entirely absent.
8. **No measurement invariance testing of the NEPSY-II across ADHD and non-ADHD groups** — striking given the WISC-V's only-partial scalar invariance finding.
9. **Publication bias and risk of bias** are not systematically addressed (e.g., via funnel plot or Egger's test) across the included ADHD WISC-V literature.
10. **Cross-cultural validity is undercharacterized**: Iranian diagnostic-validity studies (Brieflands 2025; Maherpub 2025) raise questions about generalization beyond North American and Western European populations; no panel has systematically analyzed this.
11. **Treatment-prediction validity unstudied**: no identified study has compared whether WISC-V WMI or NEPSY-II Animal Sorting/Response Set scores predict response to behavioral, pharmacological, or cognitive-training interventions.
12. **Financial and access dimensions** (WISC-V costs substantially more and requires more training than NEPSY-II) affect "ecological validity" in the health-services sense but are not addressed.

## 10. Conflicting Evidence Requiring Synthesis

A clear contradiction runs through the literature:

**Pro-WMI studies** (Tallberg et al., 2018; PubMed 42343738; MDPI *Sustainability* 2021; MDPI *Behavioral Sciences* 2025) report large or medium-to-large effects and treat WMI as a sensitive ADHD marker (https://econtent.hogrefe.com/doi/pdf/10.1026/0942-5403/a000256; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42343738/; https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/13/17/9948; https://www.mdpi.com/2076-328X/15/9/1279).

**Anti-WMI-as-diagnostic-marker studies** (Martínez-García et al. BMC Psychology 2026; PubMed 42501447; Iran J Psychiatry 2025; Maherpub 2025) report that discrepancies and even the WMI itself lack diagnostic sensitivity/specificity for individual-level classification (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40359-026-05191-0; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42501447/; https://brieflands.com/journals/ijpbs/articles/153741.pdf; https://maherpub.com/index.php/jndd/article/view/514).

**Population-level data** (PubMed 36780371) show that low WMI is neither necessary nor sufficient for ADHD (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36780371/).

**Methodological work** (Wells et al., 2017; Schwarze et al., 2024) shows that standard WISC administration under-detects WM deficits and that only partial scalar invariance obtains in ADHD samples — both inflate "no deficit" findings or complicate interpretation of WMI group differences.

**The most defensible synthesis:** The WISC-V WMI reliably detects group-level ADHD–control differences (sensory mode (a)), but its predictive accuracy at the individual child level is modest (mode (b)), and use of the WMI as a stand-alone diagnostic marker is not supported. The Kofler et al. (2020) finding that central-executive WM *d* = 1.6–2.0 when measurement unreliability is properly modeled reframes the WMI's poor classification accuracy as **partly a measurement artifact (Wells discontinue rule, partial scalar invariance) rather than a true deficit in construct relevance**. The NEPSY-II's subtests contribute incremental diagnostic value in the one available head-to-head study (Newberry, 2025, unpublished), but the independent NEPSY-II ADHD evidence base is smaller and the Gallo et al. (2025) study found no significant WM group differences on the NEPSY-II between ADHD, anxiety, and comorbid groups.

A second contradiction: Panel 1 concludes that NEPSY-II Attention/EF subtests provide superior incremental validity for ADHD detection based on Newberry, while Panel 4 concludes that the WISC-V WMI demonstrates superior sensitivity for WM deficits specifically. These are answers to **different questions** rather than direct disagreement: the WISC-V wins on the narrow WM-construct question (sense (a) group discrimination); the NEPSY-II wins on the broader EF-profile question (sense (c) incremental validity in the single available study). Both panels agree that neither instrument is adequate for sense (b) diagnostic classification.

A third contradiction: Panel 1 emphasizes NEPSY-II's greater verisimilitude as its EV advantage; Panel 4 argues both instruments share the same fundamental structured-environment limitation and that the NEPSY-II EV advantage is overstated. The current state of evidence supports a **moderate position**: NEPSY-II is more naturalistic in task design (verisimilitude), but no predictive-validity data exist for either instrument in pediatric ADHD, so verisimilitude advantages are design arguments, not empirical findings.

## 11. Citation Analysis of Influential Works

Forward-citation analysis identifies the following as the most influential works in the field:

- **Barkley (1997, *Psychological Bulletin* 121:65–94)** — foundational, >6,000 citations; anchors the inhibition-deficit framework used in nearly every ADHD–neuropsychology study (https://dconducta.es/assets/barkley1997.pdf).
- **Martinussen, Hayden, Hogg-Johnson, & Tannock (2005, *JAACAP* 44(4):377–384)** — the field-defining WM/ADHD meta-analysis; cited heavily as the source of *d* ≈ 0.47 verbal and *d* ≈ 0.85–1.06 spatial WM effect sizes (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15782085/).
- **Willcutt, Doyle, Nigg, Faraone, & Pennington (2005, *Biological Psychiatry* 57(11):1336–1346)** — meta-analytic confirmation of EF deficits in ADHD (https://www.biologicalpsychiatryjournal.com/article/S0006-3223(05)00171-X/abstract).
- **Kasper, Alderson, & Hudec (2012, *Clin Psychol Rev* 32(7):605–617)** — the most rigorous moderator analysis of WM deficits in ADHD (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0272735812000979).
- **Kofler, Rapport, Bolden, Sarver, Raiker, & Alderson (2010/2011); Wells et al. (2017)** — generated the digit-span-backward construct-validity concerns; central to the Kofler/Wells program (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5743590/).
- **Kofler et al. (2020, *JINS*)** — bifactor decomposition showing central-executive WM *d* = 1.6–2.0.
- **Fried et al. (2024, *Eur Child Adolesc Psychiatry*)** — largest meta-analysis of Digit Span Backward in ADHD; 49 studies; documented age-related attenuation.
- **Pievsky & McGrath (2018, *Clin Psychol Rev*)** — umbrella review ranking WM as the second-largest ADHD-related neurocognitive deficit (https://exa.ai/library/publication/bkyymp4jqzv).
- **Korkman, Kirk, & Kemp (2007, NEPSY-II manual)** — anchors the NEPSY-II literature (https://catalogimages.wiley.com/images/db/pdf/9780470436912.excerpt.pdf).
- **Matthews & Davis (2010); Davis & Matthews (2010, *J Psychoeduc Assess*, 74 citations)** — most influential independent NEPSY-II review (https://exa.ai/library/publication/1fs8mqkt0rv).
- **Toplak, West, & Stanovich (2013, *JCPP* 54(2):131–143)** — the most cited critique of EF tests' ecological validity; median correlation *r* = .19 between performance-based and rating measures.
- **Krasny-Pacini & Chevignard (2024, *JINS*)** — the most current systematic review of EV conceptualization in EF assessment.
- **Newberry (2025)** — only direct WISC-V vs. NEPSY-II ADHD comparison; **not yet peer-reviewed**.

## 12. Research Gaps

1. **No peer-reviewed head-to-head diagnostic-accuracy study of WISC-V and NEPSY-II in 8–12-year-old ADHD samples** with formal sensitivity, specificity, likelihood ratios, and AUC values.
2. **Insufficient ecological-validity data for either instrument in pediatric ADHD** — both lack rigorous criterion-validity studies linking scores to classroom, homework, or peer functioning.
3. **No measurement-invariance work for the NEPSY-II in ADHD samples** (the 2024 EFA examined the normative sample only, not ADHD-vs-control invariance), despite the WISC-V's only-partial scalar invariance finding.
4. **Subtest-level reporting is inconsistent**; many studies collapse to index scores, losing information about the modality-specific deficits that are central to Baddeley's model.
5. **Cross-cultural validity is poorly characterized for both instruments**; the Iranian diagnostic-validity studies raise questions about generalization beyond North American and Western European populations.
6. **Treatment-prediction validity is unstudied** — no identified study has compared whether WISC-V WMI or NEPSY-II Animal Sorting/Response Set scores predict response to behavioral, pharmacological, or cognitive-training interventions.
7. **Standardized WISC-V administration undermines WM detection** — the Wells et al. (2017) finding that discontinue rules and trial-level scoring suppress sensitivity has not been incorporated into the WISC-V research base.
8. **No identified study has compared both instruments within a multi-method, multi-informant, DSM-5-TR-framework ADHD diagnostic protocol** of the kind that would most directly inform clinical practice.
9. **Age-specific analyses within the 8–12 range are lacking**; most studies use broader age bands and the Newberry dissertation extends to age 16.
10. **Comorbidity-specific sensitivity** — whether WM deficits detected by each instrument are specific to ADHD vs. shared with anxiety, SLD, and other common comorbidities remains inadequately characterized.
11. **Incremental validity of adding NEPSY-II subtests to WISC-V indices has not been tested using rigorous ROC methodology**.
12. **Test-taker burden, examiner training requirements, and administration time** differences between the two instruments are not addressed — practically relevant for clinical assessment.

## 13. Conclusions

For clinical assessment of children aged 8–12 referred for suspected ADHD, the evidence supports **complementary use of the WISC-V and the NEPSY-II rather than either instrument alone**. The WISC-V WMI captures group-level working-memory deficits reliably (effect sizes *d* ≈ 0.50–1.06, with central-executive WM reaching *d* = 1.6–2.0 when measurement reliability is properly modeled), but its sensitivity and specificity as a stand-alone diagnostic marker are insufficient (cross-validated classification accuracy near chance, AUC 0.46–0.64). The NEPSY-II Attention/EF subtests — particularly Animal Sorting, Response Set, and Inhibition — appear to provide **stronger incremental validity for ADHD detection** in the only direct head-to-head study (Newberry, 2025) and have **greater verisimilitude to real-world executive demands** that define ecological validity in its design sense. Methodological work (Wells et al., 2017) further suggests that minor WISC-V administration modifications can improve its WM sensitivity.

**Recommendations for a peer-reviewed publication:**

1. **Disambiguate "sensitivity"** into statistical (group discrimination), diagnostic (classification), and incremental (added value) senses, because the three answers diverge.
2. **Treat the WISC-V WMI as a profile and exclusionary tool** rather than as a diagnostic marker.
3. **Use the NEPSY-II Attention/EF subtests** (especially Animal Sorting, Response Set, Inhibition-Switching) as the primary executive-function screen, with the WISC-V providing the cognitive-ability frame.
4. **Supplement both with performance-based attention tests** (CPT-3, CATA) and **rating scales** (Conners 3, BRIEF-2) consistent with current best-practice multi-method, multi-informant ADHD assessment.
5. **Report subtest-level data**, not just index scores, to capture modality-specific deficits.
6. **Use modified Digit Span Backward scoring** (counting all digits correct, ignoring discontinue rule) per Wells et al. (2017) until publishers revise standard procedures.
7. **Define "ecological validity" operationally** using the Pinto et al. (2023) representativeness × generalization framework and report prediction of classroom/behavioral outcomes to address the EV gap.
8. **Treat the Newberry (2025) dissertation as a hypothesis-generating single study, not as confirmatory**, because it is unpublished in peer review and extends to age 16.
9. **Report age-stratified analyses or restrict claims to the 8–12 band**, since most cited studies use broader age ranges and the central tendency masks age-specific sensitivity.
10. **Cite the partial scalar invariance finding** (Schwarze et al., 2024) as a constraint on WMI interpretation in ADHD samples.
11. **Foreground the Kofler et al. (2020) finding that central-executive WM *d* ≈ 1.6–2.0** when measurement unreliability is properly modeled, which reframes the WMI's poor classification accuracy as partly a measurement artifact.
